<!-- maintheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-existence}
For each $m \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant Einstein metric with $\lambda>0$ on $\sharp_m(S^2\times S^2)$.
<!-- end maintheorem-1 -->
<!-- maintheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-uniqueness}
Every Einstein metric admitting an effective isometric $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action on
\[
  S^4,\qquad \mathbb{CP}^2,\qquad S^2\times S^2,\qquad \mathbb{CP}^2\mathbin{\sharp}\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2
\]
is, up to scaling and isometry, respectively the round metric, the Fubini--Study metric, the equal-radius round product, or the Page metric.
<!-- end maintheorem-2 -->
<!-- maintheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hitchin-Thorpe}
A closed simply connected $4$-manifold admitting a $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant Einstein metric satisfies 
\[
 3|\hbox{\teneur\char28}(M)|\leq\chi(M).
\]
<!-- end maintheorem-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Two $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-actions are equivalent if a diffeomorphism intertwines them after an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$. Up to this equivalence, $S^4$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2$ each admit a unique effective smooth $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action, whereas $S^2\times S^2$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2\mathbin{\sharp}\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2$ each admit countably infinitely many; see \cite[\S\S~5.4--5.6]{OrlikRaymond1}. The latter actions are represented by the standard actions on the Hirzebruch surfaces $F_n=\mathbb P(\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb{CP}^1}(n))$, with $n\geq0$ even and odd, respectively. The following diagrams show the actions on $S^4$, $\mathbb{CP}^2$, $F_0$, and $F_1$; each edge is labelled by its stabilizer generator, up to sign.
\begin{center}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{ 
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    scale=0.85,
    boundary/.style={black, line width=0.55pt},
    normal/.style={->, black, line width=0.45pt},
    fixed/.style={circle, fill=black, inner sep=1.05pt},
    rodlabel/.style={font=\scriptsize, inner sep=1pt},
    title/.style={font=\small, anchor=base}
]

                        
\begin{scope}
    \node[title] at (0,1.60) {$S^4$};

    \filldraw[boundary, fill=gray!18]
        (0,-0.70)
        .. controls (-0.77,-0.315) and (-0.77,0.315) .. (0,0.70)
        .. controls (0.77,0.315) and (0.77,-0.315) .. cycle;

    \foreach \p in {(0,-0.70),(0,0.70)}
        \node[fixed] at \p {};

    \node[rodlabel, left=3pt] at (-0.5775,0)
        {$[e_1]$};

    \node[rodlabel, right=3pt] at (0.5775,0)
        {$[e_2]$};
\end{scope}

       
\begin{scope}[shift={(4.15,0)}]
    \node[title] at (0,1.60) {$\mathbb{CP}^2$};

    \filldraw[boundary, fill=gray!18]
        (-0.70,-0.70) -- (0.70,-0.70)
        -- (-0.70,0.70) -- cycle;

    \foreach \p in {(-0.70,-0.70),(0.70,-0.70),(-0.70,0.70)}
        \node[fixed] at \p {};

    \draw[normal] (0,-0.70) -- (0,-0.33);
    \node[rodlabel, below=4pt] at (0,-0.70)
        {$[e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (0,0) -- (-0.26,-0.26);
    \node[rodlabel, above right=3pt] at (0,0)
        {$[e_1+e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (-0.70,0) -- (-0.33,0);
    \node[rodlabel, left=3pt] at (-0.70,0)
        {$[e_1]$};
\end{scope}

            
\begin{scope}[shift={(7.95,0)}]
    \node[title] at (0,1.60) {$S^2\times S^2$};

    \filldraw[boundary, fill=gray!18]
        (-0.70,-0.70) rectangle (0.70,0.70);

    \foreach \p in {(-0.70,-0.70),(0.70,-0.70),
                    (0.70,0.70),(-0.70,0.70)}
        \node[fixed] at \p {};

    \draw[normal] (0,-0.70) -- (0,-0.33);
    \node[rodlabel, below=4pt] at (0,-0.70)
        {$[e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (0.70,0) -- (0.33,0);
    \node[rodlabel, right=3pt] at (0.70,0)
        {$[e_1]$};

    \draw[normal] (0,0.70) -- (0,0.33);
    \node[rodlabel, above=4pt] at (0,0.70)
        {$[e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (-0.70,0) -- (-0.33,0);
    \node[rodlabel, left=3pt] at (-0.70,0)
        {$[e_1]$};
\end{scope}

                        
\begin{scope}[shift={(12.65,0)}]
    \node[title] at (0,1.60)
        {$\mathbb{CP}^2\,\#\,\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2$};

    \filldraw[boundary, fill=gray!18]
        (-1.05,-0.70) -- (1.05,-0.70)
        -- (-0.35,0.70) -- (-1.05,0.70) -- cycle;

    \foreach \p in {(-1.05,-0.70),(1.05,-0.70),
                    (-0.35,0.70),(-1.05,0.70)}
        \node[fixed] at \p {};

    \draw[normal] (-0.28,-0.70) -- (-0.28,-0.33);
    \node[rodlabel, below=4pt] at (-0.28,-0.70)
        {$[e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (0.35,0) -- (0.09,-0.26);
    \node[rodlabel, above right=3pt] at (0.35,0)
        {$[e_1+e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (-0.70,0.70) -- (-0.70,0.33);
    \node[rodlabel, above=4pt] at (-0.70,0.70)
        {$[e_2]$};

    \draw[normal] (-1.05,0) -- (-0.68,0);
    \node[rodlabel, left=3pt] at (-1.05,0)
        {$[e_1]$};
\end{scope}

\end{tikzpicture} 
}
\end{center}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:curvature-conventions}
Write $K$ for the Gauss curvature of $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$, $\hat\nabla$ for its Levi--Civita connection, and $\Delta_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=\operatorname{div}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\hat\nabla$. Unless  otherwise specified, derivatives, inner products, and norms on $\Sigma^\circ$ are taken with respect to $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$. Our curvature convention is $\operatorname{Rm} (U,V)=\nabla_U\nabla_V-\nabla_V\nabla_U-\nabla_{[U,V]}$, and the curvature operator is $\mathcal R : \Lambda^2 T^ *M \to \Lambda^2 T^*M$,
\[
 \langle\mathcal R(U^\flat\wedge V^\flat),Z^\flat\wedge W^\flat\rangle
 =\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}(\operatorname{Rm}(U,V)W,Z).
\]
On the oriented four-manifold $(M,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})$, the Hodge star $\star$ gives the decomposition $\Lambda^2T^*M=\Lambda^2_+\oplus\Lambda^2_-$ into self-dual and anti-self-dual $2$-forms. We denote by $\mathcal W^\pm : \Lambda^2_\pm \to \Lambda^2_\pm$ the corresponding Weyl curvature endomorphisms. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is Einstein,
\[
    \mathcal R|_{\Lambda^2_\pm} =\mathcal W^\pm+\frac{\lambda}{3}\operatorname{Id}.
\]
Norms of $\mathcal W^\pm$ are always  Hilbert--Schmidt norms.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:quotient-equations}
A metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ as in~\eqref{eqn:polar-metric} is Einstein with constant
$\lambda$ if and only if, on $\Sigma^\circ$,
\begin{align}
 \Delta f+|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2&=-2\lambda,
       \qquad \qquad \hbox{\teneur\char28}_f(\Phi)=0,\label{eqn:general-vertical}\\
 \hat\nabla^2f&=(K-\lambda)\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}
       -\tfrac12\ensuremath{\text{d}} f\otimes\ensuremath{\text{d}} f-\tfrac12\Phi^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\mathbb{H}^2}.
       \label{eqn:general-horizontal}
\end{align}
In this case, the following also hold:
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:general-trace}
 \Delta\rho=-2\lambda\rho,
 \qquad 4K=|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi|^2-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:diagonal-reduction}
If $K_1\perp K_2$ on $\Sigma^\circ$, then $\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(e^u,e^{-u})$,
where $u=\log(|K_1|/|K_2|)$ is the arclength parameter along a geodesic of
$\mathbb{H}^2$. Consequently,
$\Phi^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\mathbb{H}^2}=\ensuremath{\text{d}} u\otimes\ensuremath{\text{d}} u$ and
$\hbox{\teneur\char28}_f(\Phi)=0$ is equivalent to $\mathbf L_fu=0$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-equations} is local: its equations also
hold for two commuting Killing fields with integrable common
orthogonal distribution, wherever they are independent.
Periodicity is used only in the orbit-area normalization.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\cite{Liu2025ToricEinstein4Manifolds}\label{lem:slice-regularity}
Near an open edge $E \subset \partial \Sigma$, choose a primitive generator $K_1$ that vanishes there and complete it to a lattice basis $K_1,K_2$. With respect to the inward distance $r$ and edge arclength $s$, we may write
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:edge-slice-expansion}
 \hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=\ensuremath{\text{d}} r^2+h(r,s)^2\ensuremath{\text{d}} s^2,\qquad
 G=\begin{pmatrix}r^2A&r^2B\\r^2B&C\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \rho=rD,
\end{equation}
where the coefficients are smooth and even in $r$, with
$D^2=AC-r^2B^2>0$ and $h(0,s)=A(0,s)=1$.
In particular, $\partial_\nu\rho=|K_2|$ along the edge, where $\nu$ is the inward unit normal.

At a vertex, the adjacent stabilizers give a lattice basis and equivariant normal coordinates give a section $r_1,r_2\geq0$ in which
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion}
\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=h_{11}\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_1^2
+2r_1r_2h_{12}\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_1\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_2
+h_{22}\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_2^2, \qquad
 G=\begin{pmatrix}
 r_1^2A_{11}&r_1^2r_2^2A_{12}\\
 r_1^2r_2^2A_{12}&r_2^2A_{22}
 \end{pmatrix},\quad
 \rho=r_1r_2D,
\end{equation}
where all coefficients $h_{ij}$ and $A_{ij}$ are smooth
and even in each variable, with
\[
A_{11}(0,0)=A_{22}(0,0)=1,\qquad
h_{11}(0,r_2)=A_{11}(0,r_2),\qquad
h_{22}(r_1,0)=A_{22}(r_1,0).
\]
Here, 
\[
D=\sqrt{A_{11}A_{22}-r_1^2r_2^2A_{12}^2}>0.
\]
In particular, the edges are geodesic, the
corner angles are $\pi/2$, and $K$ extends
smoothly and evenly to the reflected sections.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The expansions and smoothness conditions follow directly from
\cite[Lemmas~2.1--2.2]{Liu2025ToricEinstein4Manifolds}. The identity
$\partial_\nu\rho=|K_2|$ follows from
$\rho=rD$ and $D(0,s)=\sqrt{C(0,s)}$.
The remaining conclusions follow from the
reflection symmetries of the local sections.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Since the $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action is polar, by \cite{HLO} there exists a complete immersed section $S$, meeting every orbit orthogonally. Geometrically, one can think of $S$ as obtained by reflecting $\Sigma$ across its boundary edges. For example, when $M=S^4$, the orbit space $\Sigma$ is a bigon with angles $\pi/2$, and one may take $S\simeq S^2$ to be embedded. The polar group $\Pi$, consisting of the elements of $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$ preserving $S$, is then isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$, and $\Sigma\simeq S/\Pi$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:distinguished-weyl}
For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$, the unit $2$-form $\Omega_\varepsilon$ is an eigenform of $\mathcal W^\varepsilon$, with eigenvalue
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:distinguished-weyl}
 \mu_\varepsilon=K+\tfrac\varepsilon2\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi-\tfrac\lambda3.
\end{equation}
Both $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi$ and $\mu_\varepsilon$ extend smoothly and evenly to the reflected sections. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:weyl-Q-relation}
 Q_\varepsilon:=|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi|^2+2\varepsilon\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi
       =4\mu_\varepsilon+\tfrac{4\lambda}3+|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2\geq0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
On the plane spanned by $\omega_\mathcal{H},\omega_\mathcal{V}$, the curvature operator has both diagonal entries equal to $K$: horizontal sections are totally geodesic, and $[\mathcal{R},\star]=0$  by the Einstein condition. To compute its off-diagonal entry $c$, write $\operatorname{Rm}_{\alpha\beta ij}:=\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}(\operatorname{Rm}(\partial_\alpha,\partial_\beta)K_j,K_i)$. The vertical connection gives, with $S_\alpha:=G^{-1}\partial_\alpha G$ and $U_\alpha:=\Phi^{-1}\partial_\alpha\Phi$ for this calculation,
\[
 (\operatorname R_{\alpha\beta ij})_{ij}
       =-\tfrac14G[S_\alpha,S_\beta]
       =-\tfrac\rho4\Phi[U_\alpha,U_\beta].
\]
Choose a constant determinant-one vertical frame in which $\Phi=\operatorname{Id}$ at the point, and a positively-oriented orthonormal horizontal frame. Write the diagonal entries of $\partial_\alpha\Phi$ as $u_\alpha,-u_\alpha$ and its off-diagonal entry as $v_\alpha$. Then $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi=-(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$, while the commutator has $(1,2)$-entry $2(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$. Dividing by the area density $\rho$ of the vertical frame gives $c=\tfrac12\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi$. The eigenforms of this block are $\Omega_\varepsilon$. Subtracting $\lambda/3$ gives~\eqref{eqn:distinguished-weyl}.


To establish regularity at the singular orbits, observe that
\[
\Phi^*\omega_{\mathbb H^2}=-\ensuremath{\text{d}}\left(\frac{G_{11}}{\rho}\right)\wedge\ensuremath{\text{d}}\left(\frac{G_{12}}{G_{11}}\right).
\]
Near an open edge, the two factors are $rA/D$ and $B/A$, so the wedge product of their differentials is smooth and even in $r$. At a vertex, they are $r_1a/r_2$ and $r_2^2b$, where $a=A_{11}/D$ and $b=A_{12}/A_{11}$ are smooth and even in both variables. Direct differentiation shows that
\[
\ensuremath{\text{d}}(r_1a/r_2)\wedge\ensuremath{\text{d}}(r_2^2b)=\big[(a+r_1\partial_1a)(2b+r_2\partial_2b)-r_1(r_2\partial_2a-a)\partial_1b\big]\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_1\wedge\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_2,
\]
whose coefficient is again smooth and even in both variables. Since the quotient volume density has the same regularity, so does $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi$. The assertion for $\mu_\varepsilon$ now follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:slice-regularity}.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             

The equality in~\eqref{eqn:weyl-Q-relation} follows from~\eqref{eqn:general-trace}. If $J$ is positive rotation by $\pi/2$ on $\mathbb{H}^2$, then
\[
 Q_\varepsilon
 =|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi(e_1)-\varepsilon J\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi(e_2)|^2
\]
for a positively-oriented orthonormal horizontal frame, proving nonnegativity.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Geometrically, $Q_\varepsilon$ measures the failure of $\Phi$ to be conformal with the corresponding orientation. Equivalently, for the canonical almost-K\"ahler structure $\omega_\varepsilon=\rho^{-1}(\omega_{\mathcal H}+\varepsilon\omega_{\mathcal V})$ on $(M^\circ,\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=\rho^{-1}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})$, $Q_\varepsilon$ measures its failure from being K\"ahler:
\[
|\widetilde\nabla\omega_\varepsilon|_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2=\rho Q_\varepsilon.
\]
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:weyl-differential-identities}
For $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, set $F_\varepsilon:=\rho^{3/2}\mu_\varepsilon$. \label{notloc:weighted-weyl} Then, on $\Sigma^\circ$,
\begin{align}
\Delta F_\varepsilon&=\left(\lambda+\tfrac34|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2\right)F_\varepsilon+2\rho^{3/2}|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2,\label{eqn:weyl-smooth-scalar}\\
|\ensuremath{\text{d}} F_\varepsilon|^2&=\tfrac12\rho^3Q_\varepsilon\left(|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2-\tfrac32\mu_\varepsilon^2\right).\label{eqn:weyl-gap-gradient}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Fix $\varepsilon$ and write $F=F_\varepsilon$, $\mu=\mu_\varepsilon$, and $Q=Q_\varepsilon$. Set $\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=\rho^{-1}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$, write $\tilde s$ for its scalar curvature, and put
\[
 \omega=\rho^{-1}(\omega_\mathcal{H}+\varepsilon\omega_\mathcal{V})
       =\rho^{-1}\pi^*\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
          +\varepsilon\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^1\wedge\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^2.
\]
The form $\omega$ is closed and has $\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$-norm $\sqrt2$. With the orientation determined by $\omega$, the metric $\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is almost K\"ahler. Put $A=\rho^{1/2}\mathcal W^\varepsilon_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$. Conformal covariance of the Einstein Bianchi identity gives $\delta_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}A=0$, and $A\omega=F\omega$. Set $P=\omega\otimes\omega$. Since $\langle A,\tilde\nabla P\rangle=0$ and $\langle\tilde\nabla A,P\rangle=2\ensuremath{\text{d}} F$, the product rule and the Weitzenb\"ock identities in \cite[\S~2, equation~(2) and Lemma~1]{LeBrun2015HarmonicForms} give
\begin{align*}
 -2\Delta_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}F
 &=\langle\tilde\nabla^*\tilde\nabla A,P\rangle
       -\langle A,\tilde\nabla^*\tilde\nabla P\rangle\\
 &=\bigl(-\tilde sF+12\rho\mu F-4\rho^{-1/2}|A|^2\bigr)
       -\bigl(12\rho\mu F-2\tilde sF\bigr)\\
 &=\tilde sF-4\rho^{-1/2}|A|^2.
\end{align*}
The minus sign in the product rule follows by differentiating $\langle A,\tilde\nabla P\rangle=0$, which gives $\langle\tilde\nabla A,\tilde\nabla P\rangle =\langle A,\tilde\nabla^*\tilde\nabla P\rangle$. 
The scalar curvature formula and~\eqref{eqn:general-vertical} give $\tilde s=-\rho(2\lambda+\tfrac32|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2)$. The conformal Laplacian formula and torus invariance give $\Delta_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}F=\rho\Delta F$; since $|A|^2=\rho^3|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2$, this proves~\eqref{eqn:weyl-smooth-scalar}. The harmonic-form identity also gives $|\tilde\nabla\omega|^2=4\rho\mu-2\tilde s/3=\rho Q$.

At a point, complete $\omega$ to an orthogonal frame $\omega,\phi,\psi$ of self-dual forms of norm $\sqrt2$ in the chosen orientation, diagonalizing $A|_{\omega^\perp}$ there, with eigenvalues $a,b$. Write $\tilde\nabla\omega=\alpha\otimes\phi+\beta\otimes\psi$ at that point. Closure of $\omega$ and the projection of $\delta_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}A=0$ onto $\omega$ give
\[
 \alpha\wedge\phi+\beta\wedge\psi=0,
 \qquad
 \ensuremath{\text{d}} F\wedge\omega=(a-b)\alpha\wedge\phi.
\]
For the second identity, regard $A$ as a self-dual bundle-valued $2$-form, so that $\delta A=0$ is equivalent to $\ensuremath{\text{d}}^{\tilde\nabla}A=0$, and apply the product rule to $\ensuremath{\text{d}}(A\omega)=\ensuremath{\text{d}}(F\omega)$. Wedge multiplication by any of $\omega,\phi,\psi$ is an isometry on $1$-forms. Thus $|\alpha|=|\beta|$ and $|\tilde\nabla\omega|^2=4|\alpha|^2$. Trace-freeness gives $a+b=-F$, so
\[
 |\ensuremath{\text{d}} F|_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2
 =\tfrac14(a-b)^2|\tilde\nabla\omega|^2
 =\tfrac14(2|A|^2-3F^2)\rho Q.
\]
Since $|\ensuremath{\text{d}} F|_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2=\rho|\ensuremath{\text{d}} F|^2$ and $|A|^2=\rho^3|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2$, this proves~\eqref{eqn:weyl-gap-gradient}, including at $Q=0$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:weyl-sign}
For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$, either $\mu_\varepsilon<0$ on the closed disk $\Sigma$, or $\mathcal W^\varepsilon\equiv0$ on $M$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:estimateKJacPhi}
 K+\tfrac12|\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi|\leq\tfrac\lambda3.
\end{equation}
Also, if $Q_\varepsilon>0$ throughout $\Sigma^\circ$, then $\mathcal W^\varepsilon\equiv0$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, and write $\mu=\mu_\varepsilon$, $Q=Q_\varepsilon$ and $F=F_\varepsilon$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:slice-regularity} and~\ref{lem:distinguished-weyl}, $F$ extends continuously by zero to $\partial\Sigma$. The first identity in Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl-differential-identities} rules out a positive interior maximum of $F$, so $F\leq0$. The strong maximum principle gives $F<0$ or $F\equiv0$ in $\Sigma^\circ$. In the latter case, the same identity implies $\mathcal W^\varepsilon\equiv0$.

To include the boundary in the strict alternative, expand~\eqref{eqn:weyl-smooth-scalar} using~\eqref{eqn:general-vertical}:
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:weyl-full-block}
\mathbf L_{3f}\mu = \Delta\mu + 3\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\mu\rangle =4\lambda\mu+2|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2.
\end{equation}
Hence $w=-\mu\geq0$ satisfies $(\mathbf L_{3f}-4\lambda)w\leq0$. At a corner, Lemma~\ref{lem:slice-regularity} gives $\rho=r_1r_2D$, with $D$ smooth, positive and even. The diagonal terms of $\mathbf L_{3f}$ are $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}^{jj}(\partial_{r_j}^2+3r_j^{-1}\partial_{r_j})$; the mixed second-order coefficient is $r_1r_2$ times a smooth even function, and the remaining first-order coefficients are $r_j$ times such functions. Consequently, replacing $r_j$ by $|x_j|$, $x_j\in\mathbb R^4$, yields a differential operator with smooth coefficients, since $\partial_{r_j}^2+3r_j^{-1}\partial_{r_j}$ becomes the Euclidean Laplacian on $\mathbb R^4$, and the factors $r_j$ in the other terms absorb the radial derivatives. The lifted principal part is the Euclidean Laplacian at the corner, hence uniformly elliptic nearby. The smooth even function $w$ also lifts smoothly. At an open edge, the same argument applies using one radial variable and the tangential coordinate. A boundary zero is therefore an interior minimum of a nonnegative solution of a uniformly elliptic inequality. The strong maximum principle~\cite[Theorem~3.5]{GilbargTrudinger} forces $w=0$ near that point and then throughout the connected interior. This proves the strict alternative on $\Sigma$, and~\eqref{eqn:distinguished-weyl} gives the curvature bound.

Finally, suppose $Q>0$ throughout $\Sigma^\circ$. If $F<0$, then $F$ attains a negative minimum at an interior point. There the gradient identity in Lemma~\ref{lem:weyl-differential-identities} gives $|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2=\tfrac32\mu^2$. Substituting into the first identity and using~\eqref{eqn:weyl-Q-relation}, we obtain $\Delta F=\tfrac34QF<0$, contradicting minimality. Hence $F\equiv0$ and $\mathcal W^\varepsilon\equiv0$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:weyl-applications}
For the standard Einstein metric  on $S^2\times S^2$, one has $\mu_\pm=-\lambda/3$ and $Q_+=Q_-=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u|^2$, which vanishes at the equatorial torus. Since $\mathcal W^\pm\not\equiv0$, the hypothesis $Q_\varepsilon>0$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} cannot be omitted.

More generally, if $K=\lambda/3$ at an interior point of the orbit space of a toric Einstein four-manifold, \eqref{eqn:estimateKJacPhi} forces $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi=0$ there. Both distinguished eigenvalues vanish, so Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} gives $\mathcal W^+=\mathcal W^-=0$, and hence constant sectional curvature $\lambda/3$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:toric-hitchin-thorpe}
A closed, simply-connected Einstein $4$-manifold admitting an effective isometric $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action satisfies
\[
3|\hbox{\teneur\char28}(M)|\leq\chi(M).
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $\kappa_i$ and $\kappa_i^\perp$ denote the tangent and normal curvatures of $\mathcal D_i$. By Gauss--Bonnet and the Chern--Weil formula for the Euler class of its normal bundle, respectively,
\[
\int_{\mathcal D_i}\kappa_i\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A=4\pi,\qquad \int_{\mathcal D_i}\kappa_i^\perp\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A=2\pi\mathcal D_i^2.
\]

At a point of $\mathcal D_i$, choose an oriented orthonormal frame $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$, with $e_1,e_2$ tangent and $e_3,e_4$ normal to $\mathcal D_i$. Writing $e^{ab}=e^a\wedge e^b$, an orthonormal basis of $\Lambda^2_\pm$ is
\[
\eta_0^\pm=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e^{12}\pm e^{34}),\qquad \eta_1^\pm=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e^{13}\mp e^{24}),\qquad \eta_2^\pm=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e^{14}\pm e^{23}).
\]
Since $\mathcal D_i$ is totally geodesic and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is Einstein, the Gauss and Ricci equations give
\[
\langle\mathcal R e^{12},e^{12}\rangle=\langle\mathcal R e^{34},e^{34}\rangle=\kappa_i,\qquad \langle\mathcal R e^{12},e^{34}\rangle=\kappa_i^\perp.
\]
The stabilizer circle fixes $\eta_0^\pm$ and rotates the plane spanned by $\eta_1^\pm,\eta_2^\pm$. Since $\mathcal W^\pm$ is symmetric, trace-free and commutes with these rotations, its matrix in this basis is
\[
\mathcal W^\pm=\operatorname{diag}(a_\pm,-a_\pm/2,-a_\pm/2),\qquad a_\pm=\kappa_i\pm\kappa_i^\perp-\lambda/3.
\]

In the adapted frames of Lemma~\ref{lem:distinguished-weyl}, the limiting horizontal and vertical planes each contain one tangent and one normal direction to $\mathcal D_i$. Thus $\Omega_\pm$ belongs to the repeated eigenspace, and
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:weyl-edge-limit}
\mu_\pm=\frac{\lambda}{6}-\frac12(\kappa_i\pm\kappa_i^\perp)\qquad\text{along }\mathcal D_i.
\end{equation}
Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} therefore yields $\kappa_i\pm\kappa_i^\perp\geq\lambda/3$. Integrating gives
\[
\frac\lambda3\operatorname{Area}(\mathcal D_i)\leq4\pi-2\pi|\mathcal D_i^2|.
\]
Since $\lambda>0$, we conclude that $|\mathcal D_i^2|<2$, and hence $\mathcal D_i^2\in\{-1,0,1\}$.

If $N:=\chi(M)=2$, then $b_2(M)=0$ by simple connectedness, so $\hbox{\teneur\char28}(M)=0$. Otherwise $N\geq3$, and the quotient is a simple $N$-gon. The stable tangent splitting of \cite[Theorem~3.16 and its proof]{BR01}, together with the Hirzebruch signature theorem, gives $3\hbox{\teneur\char28}(M)=\sum_i\mathcal D_i^2$. Consequently,
\[
3|\hbox{\teneur\char28}(M)|=\left|\sum_i\mathcal D_i^2\right|\leq\sum_i|\mathcal D_i^2|\leq N=\chi(M),
\]
as claimed.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:connected-sum-obstruction}
If $\sharp_p\mathbb{CP}^2\mathbin{\sharp}_q\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2$ admits a $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant Einstein metric, then $p\leq2q+1$ and $q\leq2p+1$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:normalized-gram-map}
Set $\Psi:=G/\operatorname{tr}G$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-gram-equation}
 \Delta_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\Psi+
 \left\langle2\ensuremath{\text{d}}\log(\operatorname{tr}G)-\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Psi\right\rangle_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=0
\end{equation}
entrywise on $\Sigma^\circ$. The map $\Psi$ extends continuously to $\Sigma^{\mathrm v}$, taking the constant value $P_{v_i}$ along each original edge $E_i$. Each added interval maps homeomorphically onto the segment joining the matrices associated with its adjacent edges.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Choose a local $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$-orthonormal frame $e_1,e_2$, and set $B_j:=\Phi^{-1}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi(e_j)$. Differentiating $\det\Phi=1$ gives $\operatorname{tr}B_j=0$. A trace-free $2\times2$ matrix satisfies $B_j^2=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(B_j^2)\operatorname{Id}$. The weighted harmonic-map equation~\eqref{eqn:general-vertical} therefore gives
\[
 \Phi^{-1}\mathbf L_f\Phi=\sum_{j=1}^2B_j^2=|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi|^2\operatorname{Id}.
\]
Taking traces shows that $\operatorname{tr}\Phi$ satisfies the same scalar equation as each entry of $\Phi$. Substituting $\Phi=(\operatorname{tr}\Phi)\Psi$ and applying the product rule gives $\mathbf L_f\Psi+2\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}}\log(\operatorname{tr}\Phi),\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Psi\rangle=0$. Since $\operatorname{tr}\Phi=e^{-f}\operatorname{tr}G$, this is \eqref{eq:normalized-gram-equation}.

Along an open edge $E$, the matrix $G$ has rank one and kernel $\langle v_E\rangle$. Its trace is positive, so $\Psi=P_{v_E}$. At a vertex, take equivariant geodesic normal coordinates and use the adjacent isotropy generators as a lattice basis. If $r_1,r_2$ are the slice radii and $R^2=r_1^2+r_2^2$, the metric differs from its value at the vertex by $O(R^2)$, while the circle generators are linear rotation fields. Their Gram matrix is therefore $\operatorname{diag}(r_1^2,r_2^2)+O(R^4)$. Returning to the fixed lattice basis gives $G=r_1^2Q_1+r_2^2Q_2+O(R^4)$, where $Q_1,Q_2$ are fixed rank-one nonnegative matrices with distinct kernels. Consequently,
\[
 \Psi=\frac{r_1^2Q_1+r_2^2Q_2}
 {r_1^2\operatorname{tr}Q_1+r_2^2\operatorname{tr}Q_2}+O(R^2).
\]
The $O(R^2)$ estimate is uniform in the direction of approach. The leading matrix is a convex combination of $Q_1/\operatorname{tr}Q_1$ and $Q_2/\operatorname{tr}Q_2$. Its first coefficient increases strictly from zero to one as $r_1/r_2$ increases from zero to infinity. Thus the added interval traverses the segment once, and its endpoints agree with the adjacent edge values.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-monotonicity}\label{lem:two-boundary-sign-arcs}
Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be the bounded region enclosed by a simple closed curve. Let $h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric and $X$ a smooth vector field on $D$. Suppose that $u\in\mathcal C^0(\overline D)\cap\mathcal C^\infty(D)$ is nonconstant and satisfies $\Delta_hu+X(u)=0$. If $p_-,p_+\in\partial D$ are distinct and $u$ is nondecreasing along each boundary arc traversed from $p_-$ to $p_+$, then $\ensuremath{\text{d}} u\neq0$ throughout $D$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Suppose that $\ensuremath{\text{d}} u(p)=0$, and set $t=u(p)$. The strong maximum principle gives $\min_{\partial D}u<t<\max_{\partial D}u$. Boundary monotonicity therefore makes $B:=\{q\in\partial D:u(q)>t\}$ a nonempty connected arc. Set $U:=\{q\in D:u(q)>t\}$. Every component of $U$ has closure meeting $B$; otherwise $u$ would attain a maximum greater than $t$ in the interior. Each point of $B$ has a neighborhood whose intersection with $D$ is connected and contained in $U$. The component containing that intersection is locally constant along $B$, so $U$ is connected.

The Hartman--Wintner theorem gives at least four local branches of $u=t$ through $p$, separating sectors on which $u-t$ has alternating signs; see \cite[Theorem~(H.--W.) and Remark~1.2, p.~231]{Alessandrini1987}. Since $U$ is connected, a path in $U$ joins two distinct positive sectors. A portion of that path joins distinct sectors outside a small disk about $p$. Removing loops and joining the endpoints to $p$ within the sectors produces a simple closed curve. It bounds a disk compactly contained in $D$, with $u\geq t$ on its boundary and, by the alternating signs near $p$, $u<t$ somewhere inside. Thus $u$ attains an interior minimum, contradicting the strong maximum principle.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:round-s4-uniqueness}
Every Einstein metric on $S^4$ admitting an effective isometric $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action is homothetic to the round metric.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Since $\chi(S^4)=2$, the orbit disk has two edges, whose primitive isotropy generators $K_1, K_2$ form a lattice basis. By Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-gram-map}, the boundary image of $\Psi$ on the vertex-resolved disk $\Sigma^{\mathrm v}$ is the segment joining $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ in $\overline{\mathbb{H}}^2$. In particular, $\Psi_{12}$ vanishes on $\partial\Sigma^{\mathrm v}$, so the maximum principle applied to~\eqref{eq:normalized-gram-equation} gives $\Psi_{12}=0$ throughout $\Sigma^\circ$ (cf.~\cite[Proposition~5]{Liu2025ToricEinstein4Manifolds}).

Write $\Psi=\operatorname{diag}(h,1-h)$, where $0<h<1$. The function $h$ takes the values $0$ and $1$ on the two original edges, while at each added interval (of inward directions at vertices) it traverses $[0,1]$ monotonically. Thus the boundary hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-monotonicity} is satisfied, giving $\ensuremath{\text{d}} h\neq0$ throughout $\Sigma^\circ$.

Set $u:=\log(|K_1|/|K_2|)=\tfrac12\log(h/(1-h))$. Since $\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(e^u,e^{-u})$, $|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi|^2=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u|^2$ and Remark~\ref{rem:diagonal-reduction} gives $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi=0$, from which
\[
Q_+=Q_-=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u|^2=\frac{|\ensuremath{\text{d}} h|^2}{4h^2(1-h)^2}>0.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} therefore yields $\mathcal W^\pm=0$. Hence $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ has constant sectional curvature $\lambda/3>0$. By completeness and simple connectedness, $(S^4,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})$ is a round sphere of radius $\sqrt{3/\lambda}$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:fubini-study-uniqueness}
Every Einstein metric on $\mathbb{CP}^2$ admitting an effective isometric $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action is homothetic to the Fubini--Study metric.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $\chi(\mathbb{CP}^2)=3$, the orbit disk is a triangle. Every pair of edges meets at a vertex, so their isotropy lines are distinct. The corresponding matrices $P_{v_1},P_{v_2},P_{v_3}$ are distinct points on $\partial\overline{\mathbb H}^2$, and hence are the vertices of a nondegenerate triangle in the affine plane of trace-one symmetric matrices. By Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-gram-map}, the boundary map $\Psi$ traverses the boundary of this triangle once, with the original edges mapped to its vertices.


We claim that $\Psi$ is an immersion on $\Sigma^\circ$. Indeed, suppose that $\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Psi_p$ has rank at most one at some point $p\in\Sigma^\circ$. Then there exists a nonconstant affine function $L$ on the plane of trace-one symmetric matrices such that $\ensuremath{\text{d}}(L\circ\Psi)_p=0$. Choose vertices of the triangle where $L$ attains its minimum and maximum. Since $L$ is affine, $L\circ\Psi$ is nondecreasing along each of the two boundary arcs joining these vertices. Moreover, $L\circ\Psi$ is nonconstant and satisfies the scalar equation~\eqref{eq:normalized-gram-equation}, since that equation holds entrywise and has no zeroth-order term. Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-monotonicity} therefore gives $\ensuremath{\text{d}}(L\circ\Psi)\neq0$ throughout $\Sigma^\circ$, a contradiction. Since $\Phi=\Psi/\sqrt{\det\Psi}$, $\Phi$ is also an immersion.

In particular, ${\rm Jac}_\Phi$ does not change its sign $\varepsilon$ on $\Sigma^\circ$.  Consequently $Q_\varepsilon=|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\Phi|^2+2|\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi|>0$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} gives $\mathcal W^\varepsilon=0$. Since $\lambda>0$, Hitchin's classification identifies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ up to homothety with the Fubini--Study metric; see \cite{Hitchin1981KahlerianTwistorSpaces} and \cite[Remark~7, p.~429]{Derdzinski1983SelfDualKahler}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-wu}
Let $(N^4,h)$ be an oriented Riemannian four-manifold, fix $\varepsilon\in \{\pm1\}$, and assume that $\delta_h \mathcal W^\varepsilon=0$. Let $V\subset N$ be a relatively compact open set such that $\det {\mathcal W}^\varepsilon>0$ on $\overline V$. If ${\mathcal W}^\varepsilon$ has repeated eigenvalues on $\partial V$, then it also has repeated eigenvalues on all of $V$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Recall that the discriminant of a trace-free symmetric $3\times3$ matrix is
\[
\mathscr D(W)=\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)^2=\tfrac12|W|^6-27(\det W)^2.
\]
The pointwise differential inequalities in the proof of \cite[Theorem~1.2]{Wu2021} show that, for every sufficiently large integer $k$, the function
\[
F_k=|{\mathcal W}^\varepsilon|^{1/3}\left(\frac{2\mathscr D({\mathcal W}^\varepsilon)}{|{\mathcal W}^\varepsilon|^6}\right)^k
\]
is subharmonic on $V$. Indeed, the choice of $k$ depends only on positive lower bounds for $(\det {\mathcal W}^\varepsilon)/|{\mathcal W}^\varepsilon|^3$ and $(\det {\mathcal W}^\varepsilon)/|{\mathcal W}^\varepsilon|^2$, and a lower bound for the scalar curvature, all of which exist on $\overline V$. On every component of $V$ with nonempty boundary, the maximum principle gives $F_k\equiv0$. A component with empty boundary is compact, so \cite[Theorem~1.2]{Wu2021} applies directly. Hence $\mathscr D(\mathcal W^\varepsilon)\equiv0$ on $V$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:product-page-uniqueness}
An Einstein metric admitting an effective isometric $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action on $S^2\times S^2$ or $\mathbb{CP}^2\mathbin{\sharp}\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^2$ is, up to scaling and isometry, respectively the equal-radius round product or the Page metric.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The idea is to show that the metrics are \emph{algebraically special} (namely, $\mathcal{W}^\varepsilon$ has a repeated eigenvalue), and then to apply classification results in Hermitian and K\"ahler geometry.

For both manifolds $M$ in the statement, $\chi(M)=4$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:slice-regularity}, $\Sigma$ is a geodesic quadrilateral with right angles, hence has zero total curvature by Gauss--Bonnet. Proposition~\ref{prop:weyl-sign} gives $\mu_\varepsilon<0$ on the closed disk $\Sigma$ for both signs $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$: otherwise $\mathcal W^\varepsilon=0$, and Hitchin's classification, as used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fubini-study-uniqueness}, would give $\chi(M)\in\{2,3\}$. To measure the separation of the remaining eigenvalues $\nu_1,\nu_2$ of $\mathcal W^\varepsilon$, and motivated by Derdzi\'nski's conformally K\"ahler rescaling \cite[Proposition~5(i)]{Derdzinski1983SelfDualKahler}, define
\[
\mathcal G_\varepsilon:=\frac{(\nu_1-\nu_2)^2}{9\mu_\varepsilon^2}=\frac{2|\mathcal W^\varepsilon|^2}{9\mu_\varepsilon^2}-\frac13,\qquad \hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon:=(-\mu_\varepsilon)^{2/3}\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}.
\]
Notice that $\mathcal G_\varepsilon=1$ precisely when $\mu_\varepsilon$ is a repeated eigenvalue, while the conformal exponent $2/3$ produces a useful cancellation in the Gauss curvature formula for $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon$.
 Clearly, $\mathcal G_\varepsilon$ is smooth and nonnegative, with $\mathcal G_\varepsilon=1$ on the boundary by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:toric-hitchin-thorpe}. The conformal factor is smooth and even by Lemma~\ref{lem:distinguished-weyl}, so $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon$ still has geodesic edges and right angles. Gauss--Bonnet gives zero total curvature for each $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon$.



Write $z_\varepsilon=\log(-\mu_\varepsilon)$. Since $F_{\varepsilon}=\rho^{3/2}\mu_\varepsilon$, equation~\eqref{eqn:weyl-gap-gradient} and the definition of $\mathcal G_\varepsilon$ give
\[
\mathcal G_\varepsilon Q_\varepsilon=\left|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f+\tfrac23\ensuremath{\text{d}} z_\varepsilon\right|^2.
\]
The logarithmic form of~\eqref{eqn:weyl-full-block} is
\[
\Delta z_\varepsilon=4\lambda+3\mu_\varepsilon(1+3\mathcal G_\varepsilon)-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} z_\varepsilon|^2-3\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}} z_\varepsilon\rangle.
\]
Combining these identities with~\eqref{eqn:weyl-Q-relation} yields
\[
\Delta z_\varepsilon=(4-3\mathcal G_\varepsilon)\lambda+3\mu_\varepsilon+\tfrac94(1-\mathcal G_\varepsilon)|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2.
\]
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
The conformal curvature formula and~\eqref{eqn:distinguished-weyl} therefore give
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:four-edge-conformal-curvature}
 K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon}\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\varepsilon}
 =\left[(\mathcal G_\varepsilon-1)
 \left(\lambda+\tfrac34|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2\right)
 -\tfrac\varepsilon2\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi\right]\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:distinguished-weyl} gives a smooth extension of $\operatorname{Jac}_\Phi$. The remaining terms are integrable by Lemma~\ref{lem:slice-regularity}: evenness and $\mathcal G_\varepsilon=1$ on every edge give $\mathcal G_\varepsilon-1=O(r^2)$ there and $O(r_1^2r_2^2)$ at a corner. Adding the two zero total-curvature identities cancels the Jacobians and yields
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:four-edge-total-curvature}
 0=\int_\Sigma(\mathcal G_++\mathcal G_--2)
       \left(\lambda+\frac34|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|^2\right)\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}.
\end{equation}


It remains to show that $\mathcal G_\varepsilon\leq1$, or equivalently, that $\mu_\varepsilon$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathcal W^\varepsilon$ everywhere on $\Sigma$. Otherwise, let $U$ be a connected component of $\{\mathcal G_\varepsilon>1\}$ and set $V=\pi^{-1}(U)$. On $\overline U$, the eigenvalues satisfy $\nu_1\leq\mu_\varepsilon<0<\nu_2$, so $\det\mathcal W^\varepsilon>0$ on $\overline V$. Moreover, $\mathcal G_\varepsilon=1$ along $\partial U$, hence $\mathcal W^\varepsilon$ has repeated eigenvalues on $\partial V$. Lemma~\ref{lem:local-wu} then gives repeated eigenvalues throughout $V$, contradicting $\mathcal G_\varepsilon>1$ on $U$. Thus $\mathcal G_\varepsilon\leq1$.

Equation~\eqref{eqn:four-edge-total-curvature} now forces $\mathcal G_+=\mathcal G_-=1$, from which  $\mathcal W^\varepsilon$ has eigenvalues $\mu_\varepsilon,\mu_\varepsilon,-2\mu_\varepsilon$ everywhere. Derdzi\'nski's result \cite[Proposition~5(i)]{Derdzinski1983SelfDualKahler} then makes $(-\mu_\varepsilon)^{2/3}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ locally K\"ahler. The local K\"ahler forms have norm $\sqrt2$ with respect to $(-\mu_\varepsilon)^{2/3}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ and span the eigenline of $-2\mu_\varepsilon$. They therefore differ by signs on overlaps. Since $H^1(M;\mathbb{Z}_2)=0$, they glue to a global K\"ahler form in each orientation. In particular, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is Hermitian. In the non-K\"ahler case, LeBrun's classification \cite[Theorem~A]{LeBrun2012EinsteinHermitian} gives the Page metric: its other non-K\"ahler possibility, the Chen--LeBrun--Weber metric, has Euler characteristic five.

In the K\"ahler--Einstein case, $\lambda>0$ makes the complex surface del Pezzo with $c_1^2=2\chi+3\hbox{\teneur\char28}=8$. The classification of del Pezzo surfaces gives either $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$ or  the one-point blow-up of $\mathbb{CP}^2$; see \cite[proof of Theorem~B]{LeBrun2015HarmonicForms}. The one-point blow-up admits no constant-scalar-curvature K\"ahler metric \cite[Remark~7]{Derdzinski1983SelfDualKahler}. On $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$, Bando--Mabuchi uniqueness \cite[Theorem~A(ii)]{BandoMabuchi1987} identifies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$, up to scale and isometry, with the equal-radius round product.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:fixed-marking}
For every conformal structure on $\widehat{\Sigma}$ making $j$ and $\sigma$ antiholomorphic, there is a unique biholomorphism $Z:\widehat{\Sigma}\to\mathbb{CP}^1$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-marking}
 Z(p_-)=0,\qquad Z(p_+)=\infty,\qquad Z(c_+)=i,\qquad Z(c_-)=-i.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Uniformization \cite{Forster81} gives a unique $Z$ with the first three prescribed values. Since $j$ and $\sigma$ are commuting antiholomorphic involutions, $j\sigma$ is a holomorphic involution fixing $p_\pm$ and exchanging $c_\pm$. In particular, it is nontrivial. In the $Z$-coordinate it must therefore be $Z\mapsto-Z$, which gives the fourth value.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Alternatively, one could work directly with the four-copy sphere $S_\Sigma^2$, which identifies with the global section for the polar action in $M$. Indeed, the involution $(r_1,r_2,t)\mapsto(-r_1,-r_2,t)$ identifies opposite quadrants, and its quotient is precisely the conformal double $\widehat\Sigma$. The quotient map is a two-fold branched covering, ramified at $p_\pm$. Thus the conformal normalization above could equivalently be carried out on $S_\Sigma^2$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:localized-degree}
Let $E,F$ be real Banach spaces, $U\subset E$ open, and $P_x:F\to F$, $x\in U$, a smooth family of bounded projections. Suppose $s:U\to F$ is smooth and satisfies $s(x)\in P_xF$, for all $x\in U$. If the zero set $Z=s^{-1}(0)$ is compact and
\[
\mathrm D_xs:E\longrightarrow P_xF
\]
is Fredholm of index $0$ at every $x\in Z$, then $s$ has a well-defined localized degree $\deg_2(s)\in\mathbb Z_2$, with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{(Count)} If all zeros are nondegenerate, then $\deg_2(s)=\#Z\pmod 2$. In particular, if $\deg_2(s) \neq 0$ then $Z \neq \varnothing$.
    \item \emph{(Homotopy invariance)} For a smooth family $(P_{t,x} : F \to F,s_t)$, $t\in[0,1]$, satisfying the same Fredholm condition at every zero,  $\deg_2(s_t)$ is independent of $t$ provided the total zero set $\{(t,x)\in[0,1]\times U:s_t(x)=0\}$ is compact.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The idea is to reduce the equation to a finite-dimensional problem near its zeros. Since the linearizations are Fredholm, their cokernels are finite-dimensional. Compactness of $Z$ therefore allows us to choose a finite-dimensional subspace $V\subset F$ such that
\[
\operatorname{im}\mathrm D_xs+P_xV=P_xF
\qquad\text{for all }x\in Z.
\]
Consequently, the implicit function theorem shows that the solutions of the perturbed equation
\[
s(x)=P_xv,\qquad v\in V,
\]
form a smooth manifold $M$ of dimension $\dim V$ near $Z\times\{0\}$. Let $p:M\to V$ denote the projection onto the perturbation parameter.

Choose a compact neighborhood $N\subset M$ of $Z\times\{0\}$, with smooth boundary disjoint from $p^{-1}(0)$. For every sufficiently small regular value $v\in V$, the fiber $N\cap p^{-1}(v)$ is finite. We define
\[
\deg_2(s):=\#(N\cap p^{-1}(v))\pmod 2.
\]
The parity is independent of $v$: a generic path between two regular values produces a compact one-dimensional cobordism between their fibers, and the boundary of a compact one-manifold has even cardinality. Shrinking $N$ does not change the count, while independence of $V$ follows by comparing two choices with their sum. Thus the degree depends only on the original section near its zero set.

For a smooth family, compactness of the total zero set permits a common finite-dimensional reduction. A generic small perturbation then gives a compact one-manifold whose boundary consists of the perturbed solutions at $t=0$ and $t=1$. Their numbers agree modulo two, proving homotopy invariance.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:blow-up}
The \emph{real blow-up} $\Sigma_b:=[\Sigma;c]$ replaces $c$ by its circle of directions $F_c:=(T_c\Sigma\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. It is a compact smooth surface with corners (topologically an annulus), retaining the original corners of $\Sigma$, and acquiring an additional smooth boundary component $F_c$. Its smooth structure agrees with that of $\Sigma$ off $F_c$ and is defined near $F_c$ by $z=xe^{i\vartheta}$, with $x\geq0$ and $\vartheta\in\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. The blow-down map collapses the boundary circle $F_c$ to $c$ and is the identity elsewhere.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:b-geometry}
A \emph{$b$-vector field} is a smooth vector field tangent to $F_c$, equivalently one satisfying $Vx\in x\mathcal C^\infty(\Omega)$. These are the sections of the rank-two bundle ${}^b\mathcal T_\Omega$, with frame $x\partial_x,\partial_\vartheta$ and dual co-frame $\ensuremath{\text{d}} x/x,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta$. Set
\begin{equation*}
 \ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b=\left(\frac{\ensuremath{\text{d}} x}{x}\right)^2+\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^2,
 \qquad \ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\beta=x^{2\beta}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b,\qquad 0<\beta<1.
\end{equation*}
The \emph{cylinder metric} $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b$ is smooth  on ${}^b\mathcal T_\Omega$; $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\beta$ is a flat cone metric of angle $2\pi\beta$ on $\Omega^\circ$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:radial-convention}
For $r_\beta = x^\beta/\beta$, we have $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\beta=\ensuremath{\text{d}} r_\beta^2+\beta^2r_\beta^2\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^2$ and $x\partial_x=\beta \, r_\beta\partial_{r_\beta}$. The cylinder metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b$ is complete toward $F_c$, whereas the cone metric places $F_c$ at finite distance. For nonintegral $\beta$, $r_\beta$ is not a smooth boundary defining function in the fixed smooth structure. The smooth structure and weighted spaces are defined using $x$; we also use $r_\beta$ to express the cone metric and its coframe.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:b-operators}
A \emph{$b$-differential operator} of order $k$ has the form
\begin{equation*}
 L=\sum_{a+b\leq k}a_{ab}(x,\vartheta)(xD_x)^aD_\vartheta^b,
 \qquad a_{ab}\in\mathcal C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C),
 \qquad D_x=-i\partial_x,\quad D_\vartheta=-i\partial_\vartheta.
\end{equation*}
Its \emph{$b$-principal symbol} at $\xi\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} x/x+\eta\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta$ is $\sum_{a+b=k}a_{ab}\xi^a\eta^b$. It is \emph{$b$-elliptic} if this polynomial is nonzero on every nonzero $b$-covector. 

Replacing each coefficient $a_{ab}(x,\vartheta)$ by its boundary value $a_{ab}(0,\vartheta)$ gives the `frozen-coefficients' operator $L_0$, which is translation-invariant in the cylindrical coordinate $t=-\log x$. Its \emph{indicial family}, with powers measured in $x$, is 
\begin{equation*}
 I(L,s)\varphi:=x^{-s}L_0(x^s\varphi)
 =\sum_{a+b\leq k}a_{ab}(0,\vartheta)(-is)^aD_\vartheta^b\varphi,
 \qquad \varphi=\varphi(\vartheta).
\end{equation*}
For $b$-elliptic $L$, an \emph{indicial root} is a complex number $s$ for which $I(L,s):H^k(S^1)\to L^2(S^1)$ is not invertible. A real weight is \emph{admissible} if no root has that real part.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:b-laplacian}
The \emph{$b$-Laplacian} is the Laplace-Beltrami operator of $g_b$, $$\Delta_b \, = \, (x\partial_x)^2+\partial_\vartheta^2.$$ 
It has principal symbol $-(\xi^2+\eta^2)$ and indicial family $s^2+\partial_\vartheta^2$. On $e^{in\vartheta}$, the latter is multiplication by $s^2-n^2$. The indicial exponents measured in $x$ are therefore $\mathbb{Z}$, and those measured in $r=x^\beta/\beta$ are $\beta^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$. The solutions associated with the exponent $0$ are $1$ and $\log x$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:quotient-b-operator}
Consider the product conical metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\beta+\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\mathcal T}$ on $\Omega^\circ\times\mathcal T$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\mathcal T}$ is translation-invariant. Its rescaled Laplacian is
\[
-x^{2\beta}\Delta_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=-\Delta_b-x^{2\beta}\Delta_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\mathcal T}}.
\]
On $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant functions, the second term vanishes, and we thus obtain the $b$-elliptic operator $-\Delta_b$ on the orbit space. On general functions, however, the rescaled operator is not $b$-elliptic: its limiting principal symbol vanishes on nonzero covectors tangent to $\mathcal T$. Moreover, the coefficient $x^{2\beta}$ is not smooth at $x=0$ unless $2\beta$ is an integer.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:little-spaces}
Fix $0<\alpha<1$. For $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and $V^\nu=(x\partial_x)^{\nu_1}\partial_\vartheta^{\nu_2}$, set
\begin{align*}
 [a]_{\alpha;b}
 &=\sup_{p\ne p'}\frac{|a(p)-a(p')|}{d_b(p,p')^\alpha},\\
 \|a\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}}
 &=\sum_{|\nu|\leq m}\|V^\nu a\|_\infty
   +\sum_{|\nu|=m}[V^\nu a]_{\alpha;b},
 \qquad p,p'\in\Omega^\circ.
\end{align*}
Define
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)
 &=& \{a\in\mathcal{C}^m(\Omega\setminus F_c):\|a\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}}<\infty\},
\end{eqnarray*}
and let $c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ be the closure of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Omega)$ in this norm. The big space imposes no ordinary $\mathcal C^m$ regularity at $F_c$; the smooth functions defining the little space extend through $x=0$. For $t\in\mathbb{R}$, multiplication by $x^t$ defines the weighted spaces $x^t\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}$ and $x^tc_b^{m,\alpha}$, with norm $\|u\|_{x^t\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}}=\|x^{-t}u\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}}$ and its restriction to the little space.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
The $b$-H\"older space $\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ and the little $b$-H\"older space $c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ are Banach spaces with respect to the norm $\| \cdot \|_{\mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Set $Z=[0,\infty)\times S^1$, with $\tau=\log(\varepsilon/x)$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b=\ensuremath{\text{d}}\tau^2+\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^2$ and $x\partial_x=-\partial_\tau$. Let $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z)$ denote the bounded ordinary H\"older space for this product metric. The map
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        \mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)\ni a(x,\vartheta)
        &\longmapsto& a(\varepsilon e^{-\tau},\vartheta)\in\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z)
    \end{eqnarray*}
    is an isometry onto the Banach space $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z)$, so $\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ is Banach.
     Finally, the space $c_b^{m,\alpha}$ is  a closed subspace of the Banach space $\mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:little-cutoffs}
Restriction to $F_c$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear operator $$\text{Tr} : c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega) \longrightarrow c^{m,\alpha}(S^1)$$ whose kernel is the closure in $c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ of the smooth functions vanishing near $F_c$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For smooth $a$, continuity at $x=0$ implies $\|\partial_{\vartheta}^j a(0,\cdot)\|_{\infty} \leq \|\partial_{\vartheta}^j a\|_{\infty}$, for $0\leq j\leq m$. Moreover, $[\partial_{\vartheta}^m a(0,\cdot)]_{\alpha} \leq [\partial_{\vartheta}^m a]_{\alpha;b}$. Hence, the restriction map is bounded and extends uniquely to $\text{Tr}:c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)\to c^{m,\alpha}(S^1)$. Suppose $\text{Tr}(a)=0$, and choose smooth functions $a_j$ such that $\|a_j-a\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}}\to0$. Set $b_j(x,\vartheta):=a_j(x,\vartheta)-a_j(0,\vartheta)$. Extending functions on $S^1$ independently of $x$ is bounded in these norms. Hence,
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \|b_j-a\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}} &\leq& \|a_j-a\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}} +C\|\text{Tr}(a_j)\|_{c^{m,\alpha}(S^1)} \,\longrightarrow\,0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Since $b_j(0,\vartheta)=0$, we can write $b_j=xh_j$, where $h_j$ is smooth. Choose $\chi\in\mathcal C^\infty([0,\infty))$ equal to zero on $[0,1]$ and one on $[2,\infty)$, and set $\chi_\eta(x):=\chi(x/\eta)$. On the support of $1-\chi_\eta$, we have $x\leq2\eta$, and the $b$ derivatives of $\chi_\eta$ are bounded independently of $\eta$. The Leibniz rule therefore bounds every $b$ derivative of $(1-\chi_\eta)xh_j$ through order $m+1$ by $C_j\eta$. The additional derivative controls the H\"older seminorm, giving
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \|(1-\chi_\eta)b_j\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}}
    &\leq& C_j'\eta.
\end{eqnarray*}
Choose $\eta_j\downarrow0$ such that $C_j'\eta_j\leq1/j$. Then $\chi_{\eta_j}b_j$ is smooth, vanishes near $F_c$, and
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \|\chi_{\eta_j}b_j-a\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}}
    &\leq& \frac{1}{j}+\|b_j-a\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}}
    \,\longrightarrow\,0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Conversely, every smooth function vanishing near $F_c$ has zero trace, and continuity of $\text{Tr}$ gives the same conclusion for its closure.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:decay-implies-little}
Let $\Omega'=[0,\varepsilon']\times S^1$, where $0<\varepsilon'<\varepsilon$. If $u\in c_{\mathrm{loc}}^{m,\alpha}(\Omega\setminus F_c) \cap x^{t+q}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ for some $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $q>0$, then $u\in x^tc_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Choose $\chi\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}([0,\infty))$ equal to zero on $[0,1]$ and to one on $[2,\infty)$, and set $\chi_\eta(x)=\chi(x/\eta)$, where $0<\eta<\varepsilon'/2$. Set $\rho(s)=(1-\chi(s))s^q$. Since $(s\partial_s)^j\rho(s)=q^js^q$ for $s\leq1$ and $\rho(s)=0$ for $s\geq2$, we have
$\rho\in\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}((0,\infty)\times S^1)$. Writing $s=x/\eta$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
 \|(1-\chi_\eta)x^q\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')} \, \leq \, \eta^q \|\rho\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}((0,\infty)\times S^1)} \, \leq \,  C\eta^q.
\end{equation*}
Here, $x\partial_x=s\partial_s$ and $\mathrm dx/x=\mathrm ds/s$. Leibniz's rule and $[fg]_{\alpha;b}\leq\|f\|_\infty[g]_{\alpha;b} +\|g\|_\infty[f]_{\alpha;b}$ give
\begin{align*}
 \|(1-\chi_\eta)x^{-t}u\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')}
 &\leq C\|(1-\chi_\eta)x^q\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')}
          \|x^{-t-q}u\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')}\\
 &\leq C\eta^q
          \|u\|_{x^{t+q}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)}.
\end{align*}

For fixed $\eta$, set $K_\eta=[\eta/2,\varepsilon']\times S^1$. Since $x^{-t}u\in c^{m,\alpha}(K_\eta)$, choose $v_j\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(K_\eta)$ with
\begin{equation*}
 \|v_j-x^{-t}u\|_{\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(K_\eta)} \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation*}
Define $a_j=\chi_\eta v_j$ on $K_\eta\cap\Omega'$ and extend $a_j$ by zero for $x<\eta/2$. Then $a_j\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Omega')$, and
\begin{equation*}
 \|a_j-\chi_\eta x^{-t}u\|_{\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')} \leq C_\eta \|v_j-x^{-t}u\|_{\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(K_\eta)} \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation*}
Hence, $\chi_\eta x^{-t}u\in c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$. Since $C\eta^q\|u\|_{x^{t+q}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)} \to0$, we have $\chi_\eta x^{-t}u\to x^{-t}u$ in $\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$. Closedness of $c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$ gives $x^{-t}u\in c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$, so $u\in x^tc_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega')$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:4.13}
    Fix $\delta>0$, $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. The map $\left( \frac{\delta}{2}, \infty \right) \to x^{\delta} c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$, $\beta \longmapsto x^{2\beta}$, is smooth, with \begin{eqnarray*}
        \frac{\ensuremath{\text{d}}^k}{\ensuremath{\text{d}} \beta^k} x^{2\beta} &=&2^k x^{2\beta} (\log x)^k.
    \end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
On a compact interval $J \Subset \left( \frac{\delta}{2}, \infty \right)$, choose $0 < q < \min_{\beta \in J}(2\beta-\delta)$. Set $\widetilde\Omega=[0,\widetilde\varepsilon]\times S^1$, with $\widetilde\varepsilon>\varepsilon$. For every $j\in\mathbb{N}_0$, the functions $x^{2\beta-\delta}(\log x)^j$ are smooth for $x>0$ and have uniformly bounded $x^q\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(\widetilde\Omega)$ norms. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little} with $t=0$ and $\Omega$ as the smaller collar gives $x^{2\beta-\delta}(\log x)^j\in c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$. Set $p_j(\beta) = 2^j x^{2\beta}(\log x)^j$. The $b$-derivatives of $x^{-\delta}p_j(\beta)$ through order $m+1$ are uniformly bounded for $\beta \in J$. Hence,
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \sup_{\beta \in J} \| p_j(\beta) \|_{x^\delta c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)} &\leq& C_j.
\end{eqnarray*}
Taylor's formula, applied pointwise, gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
    p_j(\beta+h) - p_j(\beta) - hp_{j+1}(\beta)
    &=& h^2 \int_0^1 (1-s)p_{j+2}(\beta+sh) \, \ensuremath{\text{d}} s
\end{eqnarray*}
whenever $\beta,\beta+h \in J$. Taking the weighted $b$-Hölder norm yields
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \left\|
        \frac{p_j(\beta+h)-p_j(\beta)}{h} - p_{j+1}(\beta)
    \right\|_{x^\delta c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)}
    &\leq& \frac{C_{j+2}}{2}|h|.
\end{eqnarray*}
Thus $p_j' = p_{j+1}$ in $x^\delta c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ on the interior of $J$, for every $j \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Since $J$ was arbitrary, $\beta \mapsto x^{2\beta}$ is smooth, with the stated derivatives.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:fourier-estimate}
Let $\Omega'=[0,\varepsilon']\times S^1\subset\Omega$, with $0<\varepsilon'<\varepsilon$. Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, $0<\alpha<1$, $s,t>0$, and $0<a\leq1$ with $a<t$. If $H\in x^sc_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)$ and $\Delta_bH\in x^tc_b^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)$, then
\begin{equation*}
 \|H\|_{x^ac_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega')}
 \leq C\bigl(\|H\|_{\mathcal C^0(\Omega)}
       +\|\Delta_bH\|_{x^tc_b^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
If $t>1$, there is a unique $\ell\in\operatorname{span}\{\cos\vartheta,\sin\vartheta\}$ such that, for every $1<b<\min\{2,t\}$,
\begin{equation*}
 \|\ell\|_{\mathcal C^{k+2,\alpha}(S^1)}
 +\|H-x\ell\|_{x^bc_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega')}
 \leq C\bigl(\|H\|_{\mathcal C^0(\Omega)}
       +\|\Delta_bH\|_{x^tc_b^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
The constants depend only on $k,\alpha,t,\varepsilon,\varepsilon'$ and, respectively, $a$ or $b$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $z=xe^{i\vartheta}$, $F=\Delta_bH$, and
\[
M=\|H\|_{\mathcal C^0(\Omega)}+\|F\|_{x^tc_b^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}.
\]
Since $\Delta_b=x^2\Delta_{\mathbb R^2}$, we have $\Delta_{\mathbb R^2}H=x^{-2}F$ on the punctured disk. Fix $\varepsilon'<R<\varepsilon$, and let $u$ be the Dirichlet Green potential on $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ of the function $x^{-2}F$. Since $|x^{-2}F|\leq Mx^{t-2}$ and $t>0$, the potential extends continuously across the origin, with $\|u\|_{\mathcal C^0(D_R)}\leq CM$. The function $h=H-u$ is bounded and harmonic on the punctured disk, hence extends harmonically across the origin, with $\|h\|_{\mathcal C^0(D_R)}\leq M$. Moreover, $H(0)=0$, so $h(0)=-u(0)$.

Elementary estimates for the logarithmic Green kernel give, for every $0<q<\min\{1,t\}$,
\[
|u(z)-u(0)|\leq C_qM|z|^q.
\]
If $t>1$, the potential is differentiable at the origin, and for every $1<q<\min\{2,t\}$,
\[
|\nabla u(0)|\leq CM,\qquad
|u(z)-u(0)-\langle\nabla u(0),z\rangle|
\leq C_qM|z|^q.
\]
Indeed, splitting the Green integral into $|y|\leq2|z|$ and $|y|>2|z|$, the near contribution is $O(|z|^t)$, while the far contribution is controlled by
\[
C|z|\int_{2|z|}^R r^{t-2}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} r,
\]
or, after subtracting the linear term, by
\[
C|z|^2\int_{2|z|}^R r^{t-3}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} r.
\]
These estimates give the asserted bounds, including the logarithmic borderline cases by taking $q$ strictly below the corresponding exponent.

Since $h$ is harmonic, $h(z)-h(0)=\langle\nabla h(0),z\rangle+O(M|z|^2)$. Consequently, if $t\leq1$, then
\[
|H(z)|\leq C_qM|z|^q,\qquad 0<q<t.
\]
If $t>1$, there is an $\ell\in\operatorname{span}\{\cos\vartheta,\sin\vartheta\}$, with $\|\ell\|_{\mathcal C^{k+2,\alpha}}\leq CM$, such that
\[
|H(x,\vartheta)-x\ell(\vartheta)|\leq C_qMx^q,
\qquad 1<q<\min\{2,t\}.
\]

On dyadic annuli $x\asymp r$, the operator $\Delta_b$ becomes the uniformly elliptic cylinder Laplacian after rescaling. Interior Schauder estimates, applied to $H$ or $H-x\ell$ as appropriate, therefore upgrade these bounds to
\[
\|H\|_{x^q\mathcal C_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega')}\leq C_qM
\quad (t\leq1,\ 0<q<t),
\]
and
\[
\|H-x\ell\|_{x^q\mathcal C_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega')}\leq C_qM
\quad (t>1,\ 1<q<\min\{2,t\}).
\]
Choosing $q>a$, respectively $q>b$, and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little} gives the asserted estimates in the little H\"older spaces. When $t>1$, the first estimate also follows from $H=x\ell+O_b(x^q)$, since $x\ell\in x^ac_b^{k+2,\alpha}$ for $a\leq1$. Finally, the expansion with $q>1$ shows that $\ell=\lim_{x\to0}x^{-1}H(x,\cdot)$, proving uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:cylinder-inverse}
Let $N\in\{1,2\}$, $s\in\mathbb R\setminus N\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. On the flat cylinder $Z_N=\mathbb R_T\times(\mathbb R/(2\pi/N)\mathbb Z)_\vartheta$, the operator
\[
 L_s=\partial_T+i\partial_\vartheta+s
\]
is an isomorphism between the bounded complex-valued H\"older spaces $\mathcal C^{m+1,\alpha}(Z_N)$ and $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z_N)$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruction-cylinder-estimate}
 \|L_s^{-1}B\|_{\mathcal C^{m+1,\alpha}(Z_N)}
 \leq C\|B\|_{\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z_N)}.
\end{equation}
If $B$ belongs to $c_b^{m,\alpha}$ near $x=0$, where $x=e^T$, then $L_s^{-1}B$ belongs to $c_b^{m+1,\alpha}$ on a smaller collar, and
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(L_s^{-1}B)
 =(s+i\partial_\vartheta)^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}B.
\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Put $j=\lfloor s/N\rfloor+1$. The kernel
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruction-cylinder-kernel}
 K_{s,N}(T,\vartheta)
 =\frac{N}{2\pi}
   \frac{e^{(Nj-s)T+iNj\vartheta}}
        {e^{N(T+i\vartheta)}-1}
\end{equation}
has Fourier multiplier $(i\xi+s-n)^{-1}$, $n\in N\mathbb Z$, and hence is a fundamental solution for $L_s$. Its singularity is $1/(2\pi(T+i\vartheta))$, and it decays exponentially at both ends. Thus $K_{s,N}\in L^1(Z_N)$, and convolution gives a bounded solution with $\|L_s^{-1}B\|_\infty\leq C\|B\|_\infty$. The local Schauder estimate~\cite[Lemma~2.2.4]{Biquard2008}, applied on fixed-radius disks and translated along the cylinder, gives \eqref{eq:reconstruction-cylinder-estimate}. Every homogeneous Fourier mode is a multiple of $e^{(n-s)T}$, which is unbounded at one end; this proves uniqueness.

For the little-space assertion, choose a smooth cutoff $\eta$ equal to one near the left end and supported inside the collar on which $B$ is little. Set
\[
 B_0=\operatorname{Tr}B,\qquad
 A_0=(s+i\partial_\vartheta)^{-1}B_0.
\]
The periodic first-order operator is invertible because $s\notin N\mathbb Z$, and $A_0\in c^{m+1,\alpha}$. The datum
\[
 \eta B-L_s(\eta A_0)
\]
has zero trace and vanishes near the right end. Lemma~\ref{lem:little-cutoffs}, followed by smooth approximation on compact cylinders, approximates it in $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}(Z_N)$ by smooth compactly supported data. Their inverses are smooth and decay exponentially, with all derivatives, at the left end; by Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little}, they belong there to the zero-trace little space. Estimate~\eqref{eq:reconstruction-cylinder-estimate} passes this conclusion to the limit. Finally, the kernel formula shows that $L_s^{-1}((1-\eta)B)$ is smooth and exponentially decaying on a smaller left collar. Adding this term and $\eta A_0$ proves the assertion and the trace formula.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:compactness}
If $\delta'>\delta$, $m>k+2$, and $\alpha'>\alpha$, then the following inclusion is compact: $$x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow x^\delta c_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega) \, .$$
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Choose $\chi\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}([0,\infty))$ with $\chi=0$ on $[0,1]$ and $\chi=1$ on $[2,\infty)$. For $0<\eta<\varepsilon/2$, set $\chi_\eta(x)=\chi(x/\eta)$ and $T_\eta H=\chi_\eta H$. For fixed $\eta$, the $b$-H\"older norms are equivalent to ordinary Hölder norms on $[\eta,\varepsilon]\times S^1$. The compact inclusion $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha'}\hookrightarrow c^{k+2,\alpha}$ on this cylinder makes $T_\eta:x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(\Omega)\to x^\delta c_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)$ compact. The Leibniz rule and the scaling of $\chi_\eta$ give
\begin{equation*}
 \|H-T_\eta H\|_{x^\delta\mathcal C_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)}
 \leq C\eta^{\delta'-\delta}
       \|H\|_{x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(\Omega)}.
\end{equation*}
Since $x^\delta c_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)$ is closed in $x^\delta\mathcal C_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)$, we have $H\in x^\delta c_b^{k+2,\alpha}(\Omega)$. The same inequality shows that $T_\eta$ converges in operator norm to the inclusion, which is therefore compact.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\phantomsection\label{notloc:tensor-space}
Let $\mathcal S_{\beta}^{m,\alpha}$ consist of the $\mathsf G$-invariant tensors $H\in c_{\mathrm{loc}}^{m,\alpha}(S^4\setminus\mathcal T;\operatorname{Sym}^2T^*S^4)$ which, on principal orbits, have the form $$H=a \pi^*h_{\beta}^{\circ} +b_1\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_1^2+b_2\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_2^2,$$ with $a-a_0,b_1-b_0,b_2-b_0\in x^\delta c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ for constants $a_0,b_0\in\mathbb{R}$. 

For $\beta\in I$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$, tensors $H = \pi^{\ast} H_{\Sigma} + b_1 \ensuremath{\text{d}} \vartheta_1^2 + b_2 \ensuremath{\text{d}} \vartheta_2^2$ with $H_\Sigma-a_0h_\beta^\circ,b_1-b_0,b_2-b_0\in x^tc_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)$ carry the norm
\begin{align}\label{eq:conical-tensor-norm}
 \|H\|_{\beta,t}^{m,\alpha}
 &=|a_0|+|b_0|
   +\|x^{-t}(H_\Sigma-a_0h_\beta^\circ)\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)}\nonumber\\
 &\quad+\sum_{j=1}^2\|x^{-t}(b_j-b_0)\|_{c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega)}
   +\|H\|_{c^{m,\alpha}(K)}.
\end{align}
The constants $a_0,b_0$ are unique for $t>0$ and are set to zero for $t\leq0$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
For $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and $\beta\in I$, the space $(\mathcal S_\beta^{m,\alpha},\|\cdot\|_{\beta,\delta}^{m,\alpha})$ is Banach.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The map
\begin{eqnarray*}
 H&\longmapsto&\bigl(a_0,b_0,x^{-\delta}(a-a_0),x^{-\delta}(b_1-b_0),x^{-\delta}(b_2-b_0),H|_K\bigr)
\end{eqnarray*}
embeds $\mathcal S_\beta^{m,\alpha}$ into the Banach space $\mathbb{R}^2\times(c_b^{m,\alpha}(\Omega))^3\times c^{m,\alpha}(K;\operatorname{Sym}^2T^*S^4)$, with equivalent norms. Agreement on the overlap, the prescribed tensor form, and $\mathsf G$-invariance are closed conditions in this product. Its image is therefore closed, so $\mathcal S_\beta^{m,\alpha}$ is Banach.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:X_beta}
Define
\phantomsection\label{notloc:metric-space}
 $\mathcal X_\beta =\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal S_\beta^{k+2,\alpha}:\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}} \, > 0 \text{ and}\ a_0,b_0>0\}$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduced-equations}
Given $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_\beta$ and $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=e^{2v}h_\beta^\circ$, the Einstein equation $\operatorname{Ric}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})=\lambda\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is equivalent to the  system
\begin{align}
 \Delta_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}f+|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2+2\lambda&=0,
 \label{eqn:red-einstein-1}\\
 \Delta_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}u+\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}} u\rangle_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}&=0,
 \label{eqn:red-einstein-2}\\
 4K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}+|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2&=0
 \label{eqn:red-einstein-3}
\end{align}
on $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:ambient-einstein-regularity}
An Einstein metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}} \in \mathcal X_\beta$ is smooth with respect to the standard smooth structure of $S^4\setminus\mathcal T$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By DeTurck--Kazdan~\cite[Theorem~5.2]{DeTurckKazdan1981}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is smooth in harmonic coordinates. Let $\mathscr A_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ denote the resulting smooth structure, which is $\mathcal C^1$-compatible with the standard one. We show that these two smooth structures agree.

Consider the involutions $\kappa_j$ given by complex conjugation in the $j$th coordinate of $\mathbb C^2$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is torus-invariant and diagonal, they are isometries. Thus the $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-action and the $\kappa_j$ are smooth in $\mathscr A_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ by Myers--Steenrod~\cite[Chapter~II, Theorem~1.2]{KobayashiGroups}. Their common fixed surface is the meridional sphere $S_\Sigma^2$, away from its intersection with $\mathcal T$, and is smooth in both structures. Its induced metric is conformal to the prescribed smooth metric $h_\beta^\circ$, which is itself conformal to the round metric. Hence the identity between the two smooth structures on this surface is a $\mathcal C^1$ conformal map, and therefore smooth by regularity of conformal maps between Riemann surfaces.

On principal orbits, smoothness of the ambient identification follows immediately from equivariance. Near a singular orbit, choose equivariant slice coordinates in both structures, adapted to the common fixed surface. The transition map restricts to a smooth map on the signed section coordinates and commutes with the reflections $r_j\mapsto-r_j$. At a vertex, its components therefore have the form
\[
r_j\longmapsto r_j A_j(r_1^2,r_2^2),\qquad j=1,2,
\]
with $A_j$ smooth. Equivariance then extends this map to the ambient complex slice coordinates as
\[
z_j\longmapsto z_j A_j(|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2),
\]
which is smooth. The same argument, with one normal coordinate and an additional tangential coordinate, applies along an open edge. Thus the two ambient smooth structures agree everywhere on $S^4\setminus\mathcal T$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is smooth in the standard structure.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:cone-regularity}
If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_\beta$ is Einstein, then $f-f_0,u,v-v_0\in r_\beta^2\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}$ near $c$, for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ (see $\S$\ref{sec:reduced_equations}). In particular, its curvature is bounded near $\mathcal T$, and $K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=O(r_\beta^2)$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:ambient-einstein-regularity} implies smoothness off $\mathcal T$. Rescaled interior Schauder estimates for \eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} \cite[Theorem~6.2]{GilbargTrudinger} imply that $f-f_0,u,v-v_0 \in x^{\delta} \mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}$ for all $m$. To improve the decay without losing the endpoint $2\beta=1$, remove the quadratic term in the first equation by setting $\rho=e^f$:
\begin{equation*}
 \Delta_b\rho=-2\lambda e^{2v}x^{2\beta}\rho
 =-2\lambda e^{2v_0}\rho_0x^{2\beta}+ R, \qquad R \in x^{2\beta+\delta}\mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha},
 \qquad \rho_0=e^{f_0}.
\end{equation*}
Since $\Delta_bx^{2\beta}=4\beta^2x^{2\beta}$, the Laplacian of $\rho-\rho_0+\lambda e^{2v_0}\rho_0x^{2\beta}/(2\beta^2)$ is contained in $x^{2\beta+\delta} \mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}$. Set $H=\rho-\rho_0+\lambda e^{2v_0}\rho_0x^{2\beta}/(2\beta^2)$. For every $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little} gives
\begin{equation*}
 H\in x^{\delta/2}c_b^{m+2,\alpha},
 \qquad \Delta_bH\in x^{2\beta+\delta/2}c_b^{m,\alpha}
\end{equation*}
on a smaller collar. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier-estimate}, with $(s,a,t)=(\delta/2,2\beta,2\beta+\delta/2)$, therefore gives $f-f_0\in x^{2\beta}c_b^{m+2,\alpha}$.  Now $\Delta_bu \in x^{2\beta+\delta} \mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}$, so the same weights improve $u$ to order $x^{2\beta}$. The last equation then gives $\Delta_bv \in x^{4\beta} \mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}$; use $(s,a,t)=(\delta/2,2\beta,3\beta)$ to obtain the same decay for $v-v_0$. Thus $f - f_0, u, v-v_0 \in r_{\beta}^2 \mathcal{C}_b^{m,\alpha}$ for every $m$, including $\beta=\frac{1}{2}$. Their cone-frame first derivatives are $O(r_\beta)$ and their second derivatives are bounded. Equation~\eqref{eqn:red-einstein-3} gives $K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=O(r_\beta^2)$. The curvature formulas for the diagonal warped product give
\begin{equation*}
 |\operatorname{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})|_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}
 \leq C\bigl(|K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}|+|\hat\nabla^2f|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
              +|\hat\nabla^2u|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
              +|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2+|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}^2\bigr),
\end{equation*}
so the preceding derivative bounds give bounded curvature.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:removability}
If $d\in\mathbb{N}$, $1/d\in I$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_{1/d}$ is Einstein, then $p_{d-1}^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ extends uniquely to a smooth positive-definite $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant Einstein metric on $\widetilde X_{d-1} \simeq \sharp_{d-1} (S^2 \times S^2)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Choose the local coordinates in the branched-cover construction so that $z=w^d$, where $z$ is the conformal coordinate fixed in Section~5.1. Since
\[
|z|^{2/d-2}|\ensuremath{\text{d}} z|^2=d^2|\ensuremath{\text{d}} w|^2,
\]
we have
\[
p_{d-1}^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=d^2e^{2v}|\ensuremath{\text{d}} w|^2
+e^{f+u}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_1^2+e^{f-u}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_2^2,
\]
where the pullbacks of $f,u,v$ are denoted by the same symbols. Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, together with $r_{1/d}=d|w|$, shows that these functions differ from their constant limits by elements of $|w|^2\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}$ for every $m$. In particular, they extend across $w=0$ as $\mathcal C^{1,1}$ functions, and the metric extends continuously and positive-definitely.

Under $z=w^d$, the scalar system~\eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_w f&=-|\nabla_w f|^2-2\lambda d^2e^{2v},\\
\Delta_w u&=-\langle\nabla_w f,\nabla_w u\rangle,\\
\Delta_w v&=\tfrac14\bigl(|\nabla_w f|^2-|\nabla_w u|^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first derivatives of $f,u,v$ are $O(|w|)$, so integration by parts on $\{|w|>\eta\}$ produces boundary terms of order $O(\eta^2)$. Letting $\eta\to0$, the extensions satisfy the system weakly across $w=0$. Its right-hand sides are locally Lipschitz, so standard interior Schauder regularity gives $f,u,v\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{2,\alpha}$ for every $\alpha<1$. Bootstrapping yields smoothness.

Away from the ramification torus, smoothness follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ambient-einstein-regularity}, since $p_{d-1}$ is a local diffeomorphism. The extended metric is Einstein by continuity, and is $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$-invariant by construction. Uniqueness follows from density of the complement of the ramification torus.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:scalar-map-smooth}
The map
\[
\mathcal R:I\times\widetilde{\mathcal M}\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad (\beta,p,q,v)\longmapsto\mathcal R_\beta(p,q,v)
\]
is smooth.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Near $c$, use the multiplication estimates of Section~5 and $2\beta>\delta$: every $\beta$ derivative of $x^{2\beta}$ belongs to $x^\delta c_b^{k,\alpha}$. Along an axis, the terms of order $r_j^{-2}$ cancel. The remaining quotients have the form $r_j^{-1}\partial_{r_j}a$ with $a$ even, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-even-division}
\frac{\partial_ra(r,y)}r=\int_0^1\partial_r^2a(tr,y)\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} t.
\end{equation}
This defines a bounded linear map from even $c^{k+2,\alpha}$ functions to $c^{k,\alpha}$ functions. Apply the same formula successively in $r_1,r_2$ at a vertex. The strict inequality $2\beta_0>\delta$ also gives a smooth extension to an open interval containing $I$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:scalar-axis-regularity}\label{lem:even-angular-extension}
Let $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Near an axis or vertex, a tensor
\[
 T=A h_0+r_1^2B_1\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_1^2+r_2^2B_2\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_2^2
\]
belongs to ambient $c^{m,\alpha}$ if and only if $A,B_1,B_2\in c^{m,\alpha}$ on the signed section, are even in each normal variable, and satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:axis-conicity-traces}
 B_j=A\quad\text{on }r_j=0
\end{equation}
for each axis present. The scalar and ambient norms are equivalent on fixed smaller neighborhoods. More generally, radial substitution $a(r,y)\mapsto a(|x|,y)$, $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $d\geq2$, is bounded on even $c^{m,\alpha}$ functions, including all tangential derivatives. These assertions also hold for the big H\"older spaces.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Set $\widehat F(x,y):=F(|x|,y)x_ix_j/|x|^2$, where $F\in\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}$ is even and $F(0,y)=0$. The total-degree-$m$ Taylor polynomial at $(0,y_0)$ consists of terms $r^{2j}(y-y_0)^\gamma$, with $j\geq1$; their extensions are the Cartesian polynomials $x_ix_j|x|^{2j-2}(y-y_0)^\gamma$. Taylor's remainder estimate and the chain rule therefore give, jointly in all variables,
\[
 |D^\ell(\widehat F-\widehat P_{y_0})(x,y_0)|
 \leq C\|F\|_{\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}}
                  |x|^{m-|\ell|+\alpha},\qquad |\ell|\leq m.
\]
Thus the derivatives extend to the indicated polynomial jets on the axis. If two points are separated by at least a fixed fraction of the larger normal radius, compare their top derivatives through the axis jets, whose order-$m$ coefficients are $\alpha$-H\"older in $y$.
