Otherwise subtract the Taylor polynomial at the first point's axis projection and rescale both normal and tangential variables by its normal radius. On this fixed annulus the remainder has bounded $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}$ norm, while the top derivative of the extended polynomial is constant. This proves the bounded angular extension without derivative loss. Allowing $j=0$ proves the scalar assertion.

For little spaces, take smooth even approximants and replace each angular coefficient $F_n$ by $F_n(r,y)-F_n(0,y)$. Trace and constant extension are bounded; these approximants converge and their extensions are smooth. The preceding estimate gives convergence in $\mathcal C^{m,\alpha}$.

At a vertex use the round-sphere chart $(x,z)\in\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb R^2$, with $r_1=|x|$, $r_2=|z|$, and denote its round metric by $g_0$. Put $\Pi(x)=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} x|^2-(x\cdot\ensuremath{\text{d}} x)^2/|x|^2$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:axis-tensor-reconstruction}
 T=A g_0+(B_1-A)\Pi(x)+(B_2-A)\Pi(z).
\end{equation}
Apply the angular extension in one normal variable and the scalar extension in the other, treating all remaining coordinates as parameters. This proves the forward bound, uniformly in $|x|/|z|$. Conversely, restriction to $(x,z)=((r,0),(s,0))$ gives
\[
 B_1=T_{x_2x_2},\qquad B_2=T_{z_2z_2},\qquad
 A=T_{x_1x_1}/(g_0)_{x_1x_1}.
\]
The denominator is smooth and positive, so these formulas give the reverse bound. Rotations give evenness and equality of radial and angular components on an axis, proving \eqref{eq:axis-conicity-traces}.

Along an open axis only one angular extension is needed. Recover its coefficient from a normal Cartesian component, the other from the nonvanishing circle component divided by $r_j^2$, and $A$ from a tangential component of $T|_{S}=Ah_0$. All denominators are smooth and positive. These restriction operations also preserve little spaces.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:scalar-reconstruction}
The operator
\[
 D=\operatorname{div}_{h_0}:
 \mathcal Q_\delta^{k,\alpha}
 \longrightarrow\mathcal A_\delta^{k-1,\alpha}
\]
is a bounded isomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
In a conformal coordinate $z=y_1+iy_2$, write $h_0=e^{2\omega}|\ensuremath{\text{d}} z|^2$ and $Q=\operatorname{Re}(a\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} z^2)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruction-local-divergence}
 DQ=2e^{-2\omega}\operatorname{Re}
       ((\partial_{\bar z}a)\ensuremath{\text{d}} z).
\end{equation}
This formula gives boundedness in the stated weighted norms.

We first prove injectivity. At each point of $C$, the stabilizer contains a half-turn $z\mapsto-z$ with character $1$, so $a$ is even. If $DQ=0$, then $a$ is holomorphic off $C$ and satisfies $a=O(x^{\delta-2})$. Since $0<\delta<1$, its only possible poles are simple, and evenness excludes them. Thus $Q$ extends to a holomorphic quadratic differential on $S$. Such a differential vanishes: its coefficient in a stereographic coordinate is entire and is $O(|z|^{-4})$ at infinity.

For surjectivity, let $\upsilon\in\mathcal A_\delta^{k-1,\alpha}$. Near a point of $C$, equation $DQ=\upsilon$ becomes
\[
 \partial_{\bar z}a=G,\qquad
 G=\tfrac12e^{2\omega}(\upsilon_1-i\upsilon_2).
\]
The half-turn makes $G$ odd. With $s=\delta-2$, $T=\log x$, and $a=x^sA$, this is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruction-cylinder-equation}
 (\partial_T+i\partial_\vartheta+s)A
 =2e^{-i\vartheta}x^{1-s}G.
\end{equation}
Both sides are $\pi$-periodic, and the right-hand side belongs to $c_b^{k-1,\alpha}$. Since $s\in(-2,-1)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:cylinder-inverse} with $N=2$ applies. Cut off the datum, extend it by zero to $Z_2$, solve, and cut off the resulting tensor in the conformal disk. Doing this at all points of $C$ and averaging with character $\epsilon$ gives $Q_e\in\mathcal Q_\delta^{k,\alpha}$ such that $\upsilon-DQ_e$ extends to a $c^{k-1,\alpha}$ one-form on $S$ and vanishes near $C$.

On the unpunctured sphere, the kernel of $D$ is zero by the same holomorphic argument. Its adjoint kernel consists of conformal Killing fields. Anti-invariance under both axis reflections excludes the gradient fields and leaves only rotation about the $t$-axis; this rotation is odd under $\sigma$, so it does not have character $\epsilon$. The elliptic Fredholm alternative~\cite[equation~(2.2.5)]{Biquard2008} therefore solves
\[
 DQ_0=\upsilon-DQ_e
\]
in character $\epsilon$, with a bounded inverse on ordinary H\"older spaces and, by smooth approximation, on little H\"older spaces. Since the datum vanishes near $C$, $Q_0$ is smooth there. Its normalized coefficients $x^{2-\delta}Q_0$ have positive decay and belong to the little space by Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little}. Hence $Q_e+Q_0\in\mathcal Q_\delta^{k,\alpha}$ solves $DQ=\upsilon$. All these constructions are bounded in the indicated norms, proving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:scalar-target}
The functional $\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$ is nonzero for every $(\beta,p,q,v)\in I\times\widetilde{\mathcal M}$. Its kernels form a smooth codimension-one subbundle of the trivial bundle with fiber $\mathcal F$, and
\[
 \mathcal R_\beta(p,q,v)\in\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let $E:=\operatorname{Ric}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})-\lambda\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ and let $H$ be the trace-free part of its horizontal block. The vertical eigenvalues and horizontal trace are
\[
 E_1=-\tfrac12(F_1+F_2),\qquad E_2=-\tfrac12(F_1-F_2),\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}E_H=\tfrac12F_3-F_1.
\]
The contracted Bianchi identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-bianchi}
 \operatorname{div}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(\varrho H)
 =-\frac{\varrho}{2}
       (\ensuremath{\text{d}} F_1+F_2\ensuremath{\text{d}} u+\tfrac12F_3\ensuremath{\text{d}} f).
\end{equation}
Since $\operatorname{div}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}Q=(\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}/h_0)^{-1}DQ$ for a trace-free covariant tensor, \eqref{eq:scalar-fixed-weight} gives $D(\varrho H)=J_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}))$.

Near $p_+$, write
\[
 \hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=e^{2\omega}(\ensuremath{\text{d}} s^2+\ensuremath{\text{d}} t^2),\qquad
 \ell_1=se^a,\quad\ell_2=te^b,\qquad \varrho=st e^{a+b},
\]
with $a,b,\omega\in c^{k+2,\alpha}$ even in both variables. The horizontal Ricci formula for a diagonal metric (see \cite[\S~4.2, equation~(4.6)]{Lott2010}) gives 
\[
 E_{st}=\frac{\omega_t-a_t}{s}+\frac{\omega_s-b_s}{t}+B,
 \qquad B\in c^{k,\alpha},
\]
where $B$ is odd in both variables. Its diagonal coefficients belong to $c^{k,\alpha}$ by \eqref{eq:scalar-even-division}. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-corner-vanishing}
 (\varrho H)_{ss}=st\,C_{ss},\qquad
 (\varrho H)_{st}=e^{a+b}
       \{t(\omega_t-a_t)+s(\omega_s-b_s)+stB\},
 \qquad C_{ss}\in c^{k,\alpha}.
\end{equation}
Both coefficients extend in $c^{k,\alpha}$ and vanish at the vertex, without requiring equality of the normal and angular coefficients. The same formula gives extension along an open axis. Near $C$, their weight is $x^{\delta-2}$, so $\varrho H\in\mathcal Q_\delta^{k,\alpha}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-reconstruction} identifies it with $Q_{\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})}$, proving $\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}))=0$.

To prove nonvanishing, take $Q=2\psi(s^2+t^2)\ensuremath{\text{d}} s\ensuremath{\text{d}} t$, where $\psi=1$ near the vertex and has small compact support. Extend with character $\epsilon$ and by $\tau$ near $p_-$. Then $Q_{st}(p_+)=1$ and $DQ$ is supported in annuli about the vertices. Set $R_1=0$ and solve
\[
 R_2\ensuremath{\text{d}} u-2R_3\ensuremath{\text{d}} f=-2w\varrho^{-1}DQ.
\]
Multiplying the $\ensuremath{\text{d}} s$ equation by $s$ and the $\ensuremath{\text{d}} t$ equation by $t$ gives an even $c^{k+1,\alpha}$ coefficient matrix whose value at the vertex is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-2\\-1&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. It is invertible on a sufficiently small disk. The right-hand side extends evenly across both axes: the $\ensuremath{\text{d}} s$ coefficient of $DQ$ is divisible by $t$, and its $\ensuremath{\text{d}} t$ coefficient by $s$. Thus $R_2,R_3\in c^{k+1,\alpha}$ are supported in the annuli. Uniqueness gives their required exchange symmetries. Extension by zero and by $\tau$ gives $R\in\mathcal F$ with $J(R)=DQ$. Hence $Q_R=Q$ and $\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(R)=1$.

Smooth dependence and non-vanishing give local smooth projections: if $\kappa(W)\ne0$, use $R\mapsto R-\kappa(R)W/\kappa(W)$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:scalar-reference-index}
For $a\in\{0,1,2\}$, set
\[
 P_a^*=w\bigl(\Delta_{h_0}
                 +a\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_*,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\,\cdot\,\rangle_{h_0}\bigr).
\]
The restriction
\[
 P_a^*:
 \{u\in\mathcal U^{k+2,\alpha}:u\circ\sigma=u\}
 \longrightarrow
 \{F\in\mathcal H_\delta^{k,\alpha}:F\circ\sigma=F\}
\]
is Fredholm of index zero. Its kernel consists of the constants, and its range is the kernel of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-mean-functional}
 L_a(F)=\int_\Sigma \frac{F}{w}(r_1r_2)^a\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{h_0}.
\end{equation}
The restriction
\[
 P_a^*:
 \{u\in\mathcal U^{k+2,\alpha}:u\circ\sigma=-u\}
 \longrightarrow
 \{F\in\mathcal H_\delta^{k,\alpha}:F\circ\sigma=-F\}
\]
is an isomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
For $a=0,1,2$, consider $M_a=S^{2a+2}\subset\mathbb R^{a+1}\times\mathbb R^{a+1}\times\mathbb R$. The $O(a+1)\times O(a+1)$ quotient is $(\Sigma,h_0)$, with orbit-volume density proportional to $(r_1r_2)^a$. Consequently
\[
 \Delta_{M_a}u=\Delta_{h_0}u
                  +a\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_*,\ensuremath{\text{d}} u\rangle_{h_0}.
\]
For $a=0$ these are the two reflections on $S^2$. The scalar assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:even-angular-extension} identifies the even little H\"older spaces at the axes with the invariant spaces on $M_a$.

Near the codimension-two preimage $T_a$ of $c$,
\[
 P_a^*=\Delta_b+a\{c_1\partial_T+c_2\partial_\vartheta\},
 \qquad (c_1,c_2)=(\partial_Tf_*,\partial_\vartheta f_*).
\]
Half-turn invariance gives $c_j=O_b(x^2)$ with all derivatives. On $Z_1=\mathbb R_T\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)_\vartheta$,
\[
 x^{-\delta}\Delta_bx^\delta
 =(\partial_T-i\partial_\vartheta+\delta)
  (\partial_T+i\partial_\vartheta+\delta).
\]
The inverse from Lemma~\ref{lem:cylinder-inverse}, and its reflection in $\vartheta$, therefore give an inverse $G_\delta$ gaining two derivatives, since $0<\delta<1$ excludes all integer roots. It preserves the little spaces at the left end and has trace operator $(\delta^2+\partial_\vartheta^2)^{-1}$.

Cut the drift coefficients off in $x<\varepsilon$ and extend them by zero to the right end. Their conjugated perturbation $E_\varepsilon$ satisfies
\[
 \|E_\varepsilon\|_{
 \mathcal C^{k+2,\alpha}(Z_1)\to\mathcal C^{k,\alpha}(Z_1)}
       \leq C\varepsilon^2.
\]
Here the cutoffs are dilates of one fixed cutoff, so their $b$ derivatives are uniformly bounded. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, $(1+G_\delta E_\varepsilon)^{-1}G_\delta$ exists by its Neumann series and preserves the little spaces. Apply it to cut-off $x^{-\delta}F$, multiply the solution by $x^\delta$, and cut off again. Averaging with the prescribed symmetries gives $u_e\in\mathcal H_\delta^{k+2,\alpha}$ such that
\[
 H:=(F-P_a^*u_e)/w
\]
extends to an invariant $c^{k,\alpha}$ function on $M_a$ and vanishes near $T_a$. All cutoffs equal one sufficiently near $c$.

The flux of $u_e$ across a tube of radius $\eta$ is $O(\eta^\delta)$, since its normal derivative is $O(\eta^{\delta-1})$ and the boundary measure is $O(\eta)$. Thus $L_a(F)=0$ makes $H$ mean zero. Ordinary Poisson theory on $M_a$ gives a mean-zero solution $\Delta_{M_a}u_0=H$ with the same symmetries. It is smooth near $T_a$; invariance gives one common limiting constant, zero when $F\circ\sigma=-F$. Its remaining terms are $O(x)$, hence lie in $x^\delta c_b^{k+2,\alpha}$. Therefore $u_e+u_0$ belongs to the required domain and solves the equation, with a bounded norm.

The integral $L_a$ is bounded because its local density is $O(x^{\delta-1})\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} x\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta$. It is nonzero on $\sigma$-invariant data and vanishes on $\sigma$-anti-invariant data. The same flux argument shows that it annihilates the range. Finally, a kernel element is bounded; integration against a test function gives boundary errors $O(\eta^\delta)+O(\eta)$. It is weakly harmonic across $T_a$, hence smooth and constant on $M_a$. Only the invariant restriction admits constants. These kernel and range descriptions give both assertions.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:scalar-ambient-index}
At every point of $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$, the derivative
\[
 D\mathcal R_\beta:
       \widetilde{\mathcal M}\longrightarrow\mathcal F
\]
is Fredholm of index zero.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
For $a=0,1,2$, set
\[
 P_a=w\bigl(\Delta_{h_0}
                    +a\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\,\cdot\,\rangle_{h_0}\bigr).
\]
The difference $P_a-P_a^*=aw\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} p,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\,\cdot\,\rangle$ is compact on the spaces of Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-reference-index}. Away from $C$, it is first order with $c^{k+1,\alpha}$ coefficients; compactness follows from $c^{k+1,\alpha}\hookrightarrow c^{k,\alpha}$. Near $C$, it is $a\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}}_b p,\ensuremath{\text{d}}_b\,\cdot\,\rangle_b$, where $\ensuremath{\text{d}}_b p\in x^\delta c_b^{k+1,\alpha}$. It annihilates the constant term at the end. On the decaying part of the domain, its restriction to $x<\varepsilon$ has operator norm $O(\varepsilon^\delta)$. It is therefore a norm limit of compact cutoff operators. Each $P_a$ has index zero on either symmetry subspace.

Write $(\phi,\psi,\chi)=(\dot p,\dot q,\dot v)$. Differentiating \eqref{eq:scalar-residual-map} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-triangular-linearization}
 D\mathcal R_\beta
 \begin{pmatrix}\phi\\\psi\\\chi\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 P_2\phi+4\lambda m\chi\\
 P_1\psi+w\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} u,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\phi\rangle_{h_0}\\
 P_0\chi-\frac12w\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\phi\rangle_{h_0}
              +\frac12w\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} u,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\psi\rangle_{h_0}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
The off-diagonal first-order terms are bounded. At the axes, this follows from \eqref{eq:scalar-even-division} for the factors $r_j^{-1}\partial_{r_j}$; near $C$, it follows from the weighted product estimates.

Omitting $4\lambda m\chi$ gives a lower triangular operator. Its diagonal blocks $P_2,P_1,P_0$ are Fredholm of index zero. A triangular parametrix gives index equal to their sum, hence zero. Multiplication by $4\lambda m$ is compact from the $\sigma$-invariant subspace of $\mathcal U^{k+2,\alpha}$ to that of $\mathcal H_\delta^{k,\alpha}$. Its restriction to the constant term at the end has finite rank and belongs to the target because $2\beta>\delta$. On the decaying part, it gains weight $2\beta$. Its restriction to $x<\varepsilon$ tends to zero in operator norm, and its compactly supported cutoffs are compact. Adding this term therefore preserves the index.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:scalar-zero-equivalence}
For a metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ represented by a point of $\mathcal M$, $\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})=0$ if and only if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_\beta$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})=\lambda\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$. At a zero, the $\ker D \mathcal R_\beta$ identifies with the infinitesimal Einstein deformations in $T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal X_\beta$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
If $\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})=0$, then \eqref{eq:scalar-reconstruction-forcing} and Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-reconstruction} give $\varrho H=0$. The vertical equations and the horizontal trace equation also hold, so $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is Einstein on principal orbits.

At an open axis $s=0$, equation \eqref{eq:scalar-corner-vanishing} gives
\[
 (\varrho H)_{st}|_{s=0}
       =(\varrho/s)|_{s=0}\,\partial_t(\omega-a).
\]
Thus $a-\omega$ is constant along the axis, whose cone angle is $2\pi e^{a-\omega}$. The same holds on the other axis. Exchange symmetry equates these constants, and \eqref{eq:scalar-normalization} sets their common value to zero at $p_+$. Both axes have angle $2\pi$. Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-axis-regularity}, with $m=k+2$, gives $c^{k+2,\alpha}$ regularity of the ambient metric at the axes and vertices. Its expansion at the conical point is the one prescribed in $\mathcal X_\beta$. The regularity results of Section~5 apply. Conversely, an Einstein metric in $\mathcal X_\beta$ has the required scalar symmetries, satisfies the normalization by smoothness at $p_+$, and has $\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})=0$.

At an Einstein metric, suppose $D\mathcal R_\beta(\phi,\psi,\chi)=0$. Differentiating $D(\varrho H)=J(\mathcal R_\beta)$ and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-reconstruction} gives $\varrho\dot H=0$. Differentiating the vertical and trace identities gives the remaining linearized Einstein equations. The differentiated axis identity makes the variations of $a-\omega$ constant along the axes. Symmetry and the differentiated normalization set them to zero. The linear correspondence and norm bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-axis-regularity} therefore place the metric variation in $T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal X_\beta$. The converse follows by differentiating the scalar expressions.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:scalar-index-zero}
The maps $\mathcal R_\beta$ define a smooth section of the Banach bundle with fibers $\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$ over $I\times\mathcal M$. At every zero, its vertical derivative
\[
 D\mathcal R_\beta:T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal M
                       \longrightarrow\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
\]
is Fredholm of index zero. Its zero set identifies with the conical Einstein metrics in $\mathcal X_I$, with the topology from $\S$\ref{sec:space_conical}.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Smoothness and the bundle assertion follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-target}. At a zero, differentiating $\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(\mathcal R_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}))=0$ gives
\[
 \kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\circ D\mathcal R_\beta=0.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-ambient-index}, the derivative on $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$ with target $\mathcal F$ has index zero. Replacing the target by the codimension-one subspace $\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$ increases the index by one. Restricting the domain by \eqref{eq:scalar-normalization} decreases it by one. Hence
\[
 \operatorname{ind}
   (D\mathcal R_\beta:T_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\mathcal M\to\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}})
       =0+1-1=0.
\]
The change $p\mapsto p+C$ rescales both orbit lengths by $e^{C/2}$ and leaves the three scalar expressions unchanged. Its derivative is transverse to \eqref{eq:scalar-normalization}.

Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-zero-equivalence} identifies the zeros. Near the axes and vertices, Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar-axis-regularity} and the logarithmic change of variables give locally bounded maps between the scalar and ambient norms. On the remaining principal region, restriction and reconstruction are smooth operations. Near $C$, logarithms and exponentials of the positive coefficients are continuous in the weighted little norms of Section~5. These bounds hold under \eqref{eq:angle-identification}, which keeps the scalar coefficients fixed. The identification is therefore a homeomorphism, including for the families over $I$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:scalar-degree-projections}
Let $K\subset\mathcal M$ be compact. Since $\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ne0$, compactness of $I\times K$ gives finitely many $W_j\in\mathcal F$ such that $\sum_j\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(W_j)^2>0$ on $I\times K$. Compactness of $I$ gives an open neighborhood $U\subset\mathcal M$ of $K$ on which this inequality holds for every $\beta\in I$. On $I\times U$, set
\[
 Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
   =\frac{\sum_j\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(W_j)W_j}
          {\sum_j\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(W_j)^2},
 \qquad
 \Pi_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}R=R-\kappa_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(R)Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}.
\]
Then $\Pi_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$ is a smooth projection onto $\mathcal Z_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$. Take $K$ to be the projection onto $\mathcal M$ of the total zero set, compact by Section~7 and the identification above. Proposition~\ref{prop:localized-degree} applies with $E=\mathcal M$, $F=\mathcal F$, $s_\beta=\mathcal R_\beta$, and $P_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=\Pi_{\beta,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:global-bounds}
Let $\beta\in I$ and let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_\beta$ be Einstein. Its metric completion has diameter at most $\pi\sqrt{3/\lambda}$,  $\operatorname{Vol}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})\leq24\pi^2/\lambda^2$, and
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eqn:L2-bound}
 \int_{S^4\setminus\mathcal T}|{\rm Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})|_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}^2\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}} &=&64\pi^2.
\end{eqnarray}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, the coefficients of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}-\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_0$ in the cone frames lie in $r^2\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}$ for every $m$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_0$ is the product-cone model. Since $2\pi\beta\leq2\pi$, the metric completion is an $\text{RCD}(\lambda,4)$ space \cite[Theorem~A]{BKMR21}.  Bonnet--Myers gives the diameter bound. Bishop comparison centered at a regular point $p$, where $\operatorname{Vol}_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}(B_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}(p,r))/r^4\to\pi^2/2$ as $r\to0$, gives the volume bound \cite[Corollary~2.6 and Theorem~2.3]{Sturm06}. In smooth normal disc coordinates $z=xe^{i\vartheta}$, define
\begin{equation*}
 \Phi(z,y):= \bigl((\beta e^{-v_0})^{1/\beta}|z|^{1/\beta-1}z,y\bigr),  \qquad y\in\mathcal T,
\end{equation*}
with $\Phi(0,y)=(0,y)$. Extend $\Phi$ to a homeomorphism of $S^4$, a diffeomorphism off $\mathcal T$, equal to the identity outside a collar. Then $(e^{v_0}x^\beta/\beta)\circ\Phi=|z|$ near $\mathcal T$. Apply Chern--Gauss--Bonnet to $\Phi^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, $\Phi^*\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is an edge-cone metric in the sense of \cite[\S1]{AtiyahLeBrun}. Since $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism off $\mathcal T$ and a homeomorphism of $(S^4,\mathcal T)$, the curvature integral and both Euler characteristics are unchanged. Since $\chi(\mathcal T)=0$, the correction $(1-\beta)\chi(\mathcal T)$ vanishes. The Einstein equation gives $|\text{Ric}|_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}^2=4\lambda^2$ and $\text{Scal}=4\lambda$, hence $-4|\text{Ric}|_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}^2+\text{Scal}^2=0$. Thus \cite[Theorem~2.1]{AtiyahLeBrun}, written using the full tensor norm, gives \eqref{eqn:L2-bound}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:quotient-curvature}
The quotient metric $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ has Gaussian curvature $K<\lambda/3$ on $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Set $\mu:=K-\lambda/3$ and $F:=\rho^{3/2}\mu$. Equations~\eqref{eqn:edge-slice-expansion}--\eqref{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion} show that $F$ extends continuously to $\partial\Sigma$ with value zero. Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity} gives $K(c)=0$, so $F$ also extends continuously across $c$, with $F(c)=-\lambda\rho(c)^{3/2}/3<0$. A positive maximum of $F$ would occur in $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$, contradicting \eqref{eqn:weyl-smooth-scalar}. Hence $F\leq0$. The strong maximum principle gives either $F<0$ or $F\equiv0$ on $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$. Continuity at $c$ and $F(c)<0$ exclude the second alternative.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:density-maximum}
The orbit-area density $\rho$ attains its maximum at $c$, and $\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho\neq0$ on $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Along every geodesic starting at $c$, $\rho$ decreases strictly until the geodesic reaches $\partial\Sigma$. By \eqref{eqn:general-horizontal} and Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-curvature}, $\nabla^2f\leq-(2\lambda/3)\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$. Let $\gamma:[0,l]\to\Sigma$ be a minimizing geodesic from $c$ to a point in $\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c\}$, parametrized by arc length. It cannot meet $\partial\Sigma$, since the edges are totally geodesic and the corners have angle $\pi/2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, $(f\circ\gamma)'(0)=0$. Integrating $(f\circ\gamma)''\leq-2\lambda/3$ gives
\begin{equation*}
\ensuremath{\text{d}} f(\dot\gamma(l))\leq-2\lambda l/3<0,\qquad f(\gamma(l))\leq f(c)-\lambda l^2/3<f(c).
\end{equation*}
Since $\rho=e^f$ in the interior and $\rho=0$ on $\partial\Sigma$, these inequalities prove both assertions.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:density-isoperimetry}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathcal X_\beta$ be Einstein and let $0<s<\rho(c)$. Set $A(s):=\operatorname{Area}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\{\rho>s\}$ and $L(s):=\operatorname{Length}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\{\rho=s\}$. Then $\{\rho>s\}$ contains $c$, is homeomorphic to an open disk, and satisfies
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:density-isoperimetric}
 L(s)^2&\geq&4\pi\beta A(s)-\frac{\lambda}{3}A(s)^2.
\end{eqnarray}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Set $E:=\{\rho>s\}$. Since $s>0$ and $\rho=0$ on $\partial\Sigma$, $\overline E$ is a compact subset of $\Sigma^\circ$. Each component of $E$ contains an interior maximum of $\rho$, hence contains $c$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:density-maximum}. Any component of $\Sigma\setminus E$ disjoint from $\partial\Sigma$ would contain an interior minimum away from $c$, contradicting the same lemma. Thus $E$ is a disk. Since $\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho\neq0$ on $\partial E$, its boundary is a smooth simple closed curve. Choose a domain $\Omega$ with smooth boundary and $E\Subset\Omega\Subset\Sigma^\circ$, and a conformal coordinate $z$ on $\Omega$ with $z(c)=0$. Near $c$, write $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=|z|^{2\beta-2}e^{2v}|\ensuremath{\text{d}} z|^2$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, $v-v_0\in |z|^{2\beta}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}$ for every $m$. Hence
\begin{equation*}
 \left|\int_{|z|=\eta}\partial_\nu v\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\ell\right|  \leq C\eta^{2\beta}\longrightarrow0,
\end{equation*}
where $\nu$ and $\ensuremath{\text{d}}\ell$ are the Euclidean unit normal and arc length. The curvature measure is therefore $K\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}+2\pi(1-\beta)\delta_c$. The curvature measure has finite total variation on $\Omega$. Its only atom is at $c$, with mass $2\pi(1-\beta)<2\pi$. Let $\kappa$ denote the curvature measure above. Writing $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=e^{2u}|\ensuremath{\text{d}} z|^2$, we have
\begin{equation*}
 u(z)=h(z)+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_\Omega
 \log\frac{1}{|z-\zeta|}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\kappa(\zeta),
\end{equation*}
where $h$ is harmonic. In the conventions of~\cite[Definition~4.1]{BartolucciCastorina2019}, the conformal exponent and representing measure are $2u$ and $2\kappa$. The bound $\kappa(\{c\})=2\pi(1-\beta)<2\pi$ is precisely the no-cusp condition in~\cite[Remark~4.3]{BartolucciCastorina2019}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-curvature}, $K\leq\lambda/3$, so
\begin{equation*}
 \sup_{\substack{B\subset E\\ B\ \mathrm{Borel}}} \left(\kappa(B)-\frac{\lambda}{3} \operatorname{Area}_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}(B)\right)  =2\pi(1-\beta).
\end{equation*}
The supremum is attained at $B=\{c\}$. Applying \cite[Theorem~4.7, equation~(4.9)]{BartolucciCastorina2019} with $K_0=\lambda/3$ gives \eqref{eq:density-isoperimetric}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:density}
Orient $E_1,E_2$ by the boundary orientation of $\Sigma$. Then
\begin{eqnarray}
 P=P(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})&:=&\frac{\lambda\text{Vol}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})}{2\pi^2}
 =-2\int_{E_1} \star_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho
 =-2\int_{E_2} \star_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho,
 \label{eq:density-boundary}\\
 \sup_\Sigma\rho&\leq&\frac{\sqrt3}{4\pi\beta}P
 \leq\frac{\sqrt3}{4\pi\beta_0}P.
 \label{eq:density-bound}
\end{eqnarray}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Integrating~\eqref{eqn:general-trace} over $\Sigma$ and using
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:orbit-volume}
    \operatorname{Vol}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})
    =4\pi^2\int_\Sigma\rho\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}
\end{equation}
(see~\eqref{eq:conical-ansatz}) gives
\begin{equation*}
 -\int_{\partial\Sigma}\star_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho =2\lambda\int_\Sigma\rho\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}=P.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity}, $|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\leq Cr$ near $c$, so $\int_{\{r=\eta\}} \star_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho\to0$ as $\eta\to0$. The symmetry exchanging $E_1$ and $E_2$ gives $-\int_{E_i} \star_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho=P/2$ for $i=1,2$, proving \eqref{eq:density-boundary}. Set $M:=\rho(c)$ and let $A,L$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:density-isoperimetry}. Define
\begin{equation*}
H(A(s)):=\int_{\{\rho>s\}}\rho\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}, \qquad 0<s<M.
\end{equation*}
The coarea formula gives $A'(s)<0$ and $\frac{\ensuremath{\text{d}}}{\ensuremath{\text{d}} s}H(A(s))=sA'(s)$. Hence $H'(A(s))=s$ and $H''(A(s))=1/A'(s)<0$. Set $a:=A(s)$. Stokes' theorem gives $\int_{\{\rho=s\}}|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\rho|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\ell_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}} =2\lambda H(a)$. Cauchy--Schwarz and Lemma~\ref{lem:density-isoperimetry} then give
\begin{eqnarray*}
 4\pi\beta a-\frac{\lambda}{3}a^2 \leq L(s)^2 \leq2\lambda H(a)(-A'(s)) =-\frac{2\lambda H(a)}{H''(a)}.
\end{eqnarray*}
Where $4\pi\beta a-\lambda a^2/3>0$, this gives
\begin{equation*}
 H''(a)+\frac{2\lambda H(a)}  {4\pi\beta a-\lambda a^2/3}\geq0.
\end{equation*}
The extension to $a=0$ satisfies $H(0)=0$ and $H'(0)=M$. The function
\begin{eqnarray*}
 H_0(a)&=&\frac{12\pi\beta M}{\lambda}y(1-y)(1-2y),  \qquad y=\frac{\lambda a}{12\pi\beta},
\end{eqnarray*}
satisfies $H_0''+2\lambda H_0/(4\pi\beta a-\lambda a^2/3)=0$, with $H_0(0)=0$ and $H_0'(0)=M$. The derivative $H_0'$ first vanishes at $a_*:=(2\pi\beta/\lambda)(3-\sqrt3)$. Set $W:=H'H_0-HH_0'$. For $0<a<\min\{a_*,A(0)\}$, we have $H_0>0$ and $W'\geq0$. Since $W\to0$ and $H/H_0\to1$ as $a\to0$, it follows that $H\geq H_0$ and $H'\geq(H/H_0)H_0'\geq H_0'>0$. If $A(0)<a_*$, taking $a\uparrow A(0)$ would contradict $H'(A(0))=0$. Thus $A(0)\geq a_*$. Since $H$ is increasing,
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{P}{2\lambda} =H(A(0))\geq H(a_*)\geq H_0(a_*)  =\frac{2\pi\beta M}{\sqrt3\lambda}.
\end{equation*}
This gives \eqref{eq:density-bound}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:properness-static-field}
A complete Ricci-flat four-manifold is flat if it admits a nowhere-zero Killing field whose orthogonal distribution is integrable.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let $Z$ be the nowhere-zero Killing field. The second fundamental form of each leaf of $Z^\perp$ is symmetric and, by the Killing equation, skew-symmetric. It therefore vanishes, so each leaf is totally geodesic. An ambient geodesic initially tangent to a leaf remains in it, since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}(Z,\dot\gamma)$ is constant. Completeness of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ therefore implies completeness of each leaf. Extend local coordinates on a leaf along the flow of $Z$, with parameter $t$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=g_3+N^2\ensuremath{\text{d}} t^2$, where $g_3$ is the induced leaf metric and $N:=|Z|_\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}>0$. Since $Z$ is Killing, $g_3$ and $N$ are independent of $t$. Ricci flatness gives
\begin{equation*}
 \Delta_{g_3}N=0,\qquad  N\text{Ric}_{g_3}=\nabla^2_{g_3}N.
\end{equation*}
Anderson's static-vacuum estimate~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{Anderson00}, together with completeness of the leaf and positivity of $N$, gives $\text{Ric}_{g_3}=0$ and $\ensuremath{\text{d}} N=0$. Since a three-dimensional Ricci-flat metric is flat and $N$ is constant, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}=g_3+N^2\ensuremath{\text{d}} t^2$ is flat.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:properness-marked-action}
Let $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,p_i)\to(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty,p)$ smoothly, with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i$ in the diagonal family and uniformly bounded curvature. Suppose $X$ is complete, nonflat, and Ricci-flat, and $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,\mathcal T)\to\infty$. Then each fixed circle generator vanishes within a uniformly bounded distance of $p_i$. Along a subsequence, the $T^2$-actions converge smoothly, with the same stabilizers and edge labels.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Write $K_{i,1},K_{i,2}$ for the fixed circle generators. Suppose, along a subsequence, that $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,\{K_{i,a}=0\})\to\infty$ for some $a\in\{1,2\}$. On a unit ball at distance at least one from $\{K_{i,a}=0\}$, $N_{i,a}:=|K_{i,a}|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}>0$. Along unit-speed geodesics orthogonal to $K_{i,a}$, the curvature bound gives $|N_{i,a}''|\leq C N_{i,a}$. At the center of the ball, comparison with $u''=Cu$ in both directions gives the first estimate; the diagonal form gives the second:
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:positive-jacobi-bound}
|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\log N_{i,a}|&\leq&\sqrt C\coth\sqrt C, \qquad |\nabla K_{i,a}|^2=2|\ensuremath{\text{d}} N_{i,a}|^2.
\end{eqnarray}
These bounds and $|\nabla^2K_{i,a}|\leq C|\text{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|\,|K_{i,a}|$ give, along a subsequence, smooth convergence of $K_{i,a}/N_{i,a}(p_i)$ on compact sets to a nowhere-zero Killing field with integrable orthogonal distribution. Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-static-field} then forces $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty$ to be flat, a contradiction. Each generator has a zero within a uniformly bounded distance of $p_i$. Its circle rotates the normal plane with period $2\pi$, so $|\nabla K_{i,a}|^2=2$ at its zeros. Integrating $|\nabla^2K_{i,a}|\leq C|K_{i,a}|$ along geodesics from these zeros to $p_i$ gives $c\leq |K_{i,a}(p_i)|+|\nabla K_{i,a}(p_i)|\leq C$, where $c,C>0$ are independent of $i$. At a limiting zero, the differential of the time-$t$ flow rotates the normal plane through angle $t$. Thus any positive period is a multiple of $2\pi$, so $2\pi$ is the minimal period. Let $\Phi_i$ be the convergence embeddings on relatively compact invariant domains. Following the center-of-mass construction of~\cite{GroveKarcher1973}, consider the points $a\Phi_i(a^{-1}x)$, $a\in T^2$. For large $i$, they lie in a small convex normal ball about $\Phi_i(x)$. Their center of mass for Haar probability measure defines a smooth map $F_i$. Haar invariance and the isometric action give $F_i(ax)=aF_i(x)$. Since $F_i$ is $\mathcal C^1$-close to $\Phi_i$, it is an embedding on a smaller invariant domain. Injectivity gives $\text{Stab}_{T^2}(x)=\text{Stab}_{T^2}(F_i(x))$. Thus the limiting action is effective and has the same edge labels.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:properness-one-corner}
Let $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}})$ be a complete diagonal Ricci-flat four-manifold with an effective $T^2$-action and no nontrivial finite stabilizers. Suppose the quotient of the free orbits is simply connected and $\partial(X/T^2)$ consists of two smooth edges meeting at one smooth corner. Let $h$ be the quotient metric. If $K_h\leq0$, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}$ is flat.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Set $R:=\rho$. Since $\lambda=0$ and $K_h\leq0$, equations~\eqref{eqn:general-trace} and~\eqref{eqn:general-horizontal} give $\Delta_hR=0$ and $\nabla_h^2\log R\leq0$. If $\ensuremath{\text{d}} R(q)=0$, then along each geodesic $\gamma$ starting at $q$, $(\log R\circ\gamma)'(0)=0$ and $(\log R\circ\gamma)''\leq0$. Thus $R\leq R(q)$ near $q$. The maximum principle makes $R$ constant, contradicting $R>0$ in the interior and $R=0$ on the boundary. Hence $\ensuremath{\text{d}} R\neq0$. Since $\ensuremath{\text{d}}(\star_h\ensuremath{\text{d}} R)=(\Delta_hR)\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_h=0$, the form $\star_h\ensuremath{\text{d}} R$ is closed. Simply connectedness makes it exact; choose $z$ with $\ensuremath{\text{d}} z=-\star_h\ensuremath{\text{d}} R$. In the local coordinates $(R,z)$, write $h=e^{2\nu}(\ensuremath{\text{d}} R^2+\ensuremath{\text{d}} z^2)$. Equation~\eqref{eqn:general-trace}, Remark~\ref{rem:diagonal-reduction}, and $K_h\leq0$ give the first estimate below; the horizontal equation gives the remaining identities:
\begin{eqnarray*}
u_R^2+u_z^2&\leq&R^{-2},\\
\nu_R&=&\frac R4(u_R^2-u_z^2)-\frac1{4R},\qquad \nu_z=\frac R2u_Ru_z.
\end{eqnarray*}
Set $F:=(R,z)$. Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb R_{>0}\times\mathbb R$ be piecewise smooth and put $r_0:=\min_\gamma R>0$. If $\tilde\gamma$ is a lift of $\gamma$ defined on $[0,T)$, then for $0\leq t<T$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
|\nu(\tilde\gamma(t))-\nu(\tilde\gamma(0))|
&\leq&\frac{\sqrt5}{4r_0}
\operatorname{Length}_{\mathbb R^2}(\gamma).
\end{eqnarray*}
The upper bound for $\nu$ gives finite $h$-length for $\tilde\gamma$, so completeness of the quotient gives a limit $q$ as $t\uparrow T$. Since $R(q)=R(\gamma(T))>0$ and there are no exceptional orbits, $q$ is principal. Hence $F(q)=\gamma(T)$, and the local inverse of $F$ continues the lift. Every lift therefore extends to its endpoint. Lifting segments from a point of $F$'s image shows that $F$ is onto. For a ball $B\Subset\mathbb R_{>0}\times\mathbb R$ centered at $y$, lifting radial segments from each point of $F^{-1}(y)$ defines inverse branches over $B$. Uniqueness of lifts makes their images disjoint; lifting the reversed segments shows that they exhaust $F^{-1}(B)$. Thus $F$ is a covering of the simply connected half-plane $\mathbb R_{>0}\times\mathbb R$, and hence a diffeomorphism. For fixed $z$, integrating $\nu_R\geq-1/(2R)$ gives $e^\nu\leq CR^{-1/2}$, so $\int_0^{R_0}e^{\nu(R,z)}\ensuremath{\text{d}} R\leq2C\sqrt{R_0}<\infty$. Near an open edge, \eqref{eqn:edge-slice-expansion} gives $R=rD$ with $D(0,s)>0$. The closed form $\star_h\ensuremath{\text{d}} R$ extends smoothly to the edge, so its primitive $z$ does too. The extended functions $(R,z)$ are local coordinates there:
\begin{eqnarray*}
\left|\det\frac{\partial(R,z)}{\partial(r,s)}\right|_{r=0} &=&D(0,s)^2>0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Normalize $z$ to vanish at the corner. With the chosen sign of $\ensuremath{\text{d}} z$, the function $z+iR$ is holomorphic. After reflection across both edges, \eqref{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion} gives it a double zero at the corner. Choose $x+iy:=\sqrt{2(z+iR)}$ with $x,y>0$ in the interior; this defines smooth coordinates at the corner. Then $R=xy$ and $z=(x^2-y^2)/2$, with the edges on the positive coordinate axes. For the flat metric, $u_0=\log(x/y)$ and $e^{2\nu_0}=(2\sqrt{R^2+z^2})^{-1}$. The difference $w:=u-u_0$ satisfies $w_{RR}+R^{-1}w_R+w_{zz}=0$. Thus $(\xi,\eta,z)\mapsto w(\sqrt{\xi^2+\eta^2},z)$ is harmonic on $\mathbb R^3$ away from the $z$-axis. Equations~\eqref{eqn:edge-slice-expansion} and~\eqref{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion} show that $w$ extends smoothly across the $z$-axis away from the origin and is bounded at the origin. Hence $w$ extends harmonically to $\mathbb R^3$. Since $|\nabla w|\leq2/R$, the mean-value property applied to $\partial_z w$ gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
|\partial_zw(p)|\leq\frac2{|B_L|} \int_{B_L(p)}R^{-1}\leq\frac CL\longrightarrow0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Thus $w_z=0$ and $(Rw_R)_R=0$. Smoothness at $R=0$ gives $w=B$. The formulas for $\nu_R,\nu_z$ give $\nu=\nu_0+C$. In $(x,y)$ coordinates, $h=e^{2C}(\ensuremath{\text{d}} x^2+\ensuremath{\text{d}} y^2)$, $G_{11}=e^Bx^2$ and $G_{22}=e^{-B}y^2$. Smoothness at $x=0$ and $y=0$, with minimal circle periods $2\pi$, gives $e^B=e^{2C}=e^{-B}$, so $B=C=0$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:polarbubbles}
Let $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,p_i)$ in the diagonal family, with fixed circle generators, converge smoothly to a complete nonflat Ricci-flat limit $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty,p)$. Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty$ has bounded curvature, $K_h\leq0$, and $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,\mathcal T)\to\infty$. Then $X/T^2$ contains a compact edge that, for large $i$, the embeddings of Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-marked-action} map onto an entire original edge, including both endpoints and with the same stabilizer circle.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-marked-action}, each compact subset of $\Sigma$ embeds in the original quotient disk, preserving stabilizers and edge labels. Thus $\Sigma$ has genus zero, no nontrivial finite stabilizers, and at most two corners. Moreover, $\Sigma$ is noncompact. Otherwise $X$ would be compact, and Bochner's formula would make both generators parallel. Their independence on the free orbits gives a local product $\mathbb R^2\times N$, where $N$ is a Ricci-flat surface. Since $N$ is flat, $X$ would be flat, a contradiction. Also, $\Sigma$ has one end. Otherwise $X$ would have more than one end, since $\ensuremath{\mathsf{T}^2}$ is compact. The splitting theorem~\cite{CheegerGromoll71} would give $X\cong\mathbb R\times Y$ isometrically, with $Y$ a Ricci-flat three-manifold. Then $Y$, and hence $X$, would be flat, a contradiction.

A circular boundary component $C\subset\partial\Sigma$ without corners would embed in an original edge interval, which is impossible. If $C$ had one corner $q$, then $C\setminus\{q\}$ would be connected with constant stabilizer, so the stabilizers on both sides of $q$ would agree, contrary to~\eqref{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion}. Thus $C$ has two corners, joined by a compact edge $E$. Otherwise every boundary component is a line. Since $\Sigma$ has genus zero and one end, each simple closed curve in $\Sigma^\circ$ bounds a compact region. That region contains no boundary line and is therefore a disk. Hence $\pi_1(\Sigma^\circ)=0$. An arc meeting $\partial\Sigma$ only at endpoints on two distinct lines would separate $\Sigma$ into two noncompact components, contradicting its single end. Thus there is at most one boundary line. If $\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ or the line had no corners, one fixed circle generator would be nowhere zero, making $X$ flat by Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-static-field}. Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-one-corner} excludes one corner. Hence the boundary line has two corners, joined by a compact edge $E$.

Let $E_i$ be the original edge with the same label as $E$. For large $i$, Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-marked-action} gives a quotient embedding $\bar F_i$ with $\bar F_i(E)\subset E_i$ and $\bar F_i(\partial E)=\partial E_i$. Since $\bar F_i(E)$ is connected, $\bar F_i(E)=E_i$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- notation-2: body_md -->
\label{not:rescaled-covers}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i\in\mathcal X_{\beta_i}$ be Einstein, with $\beta_i\in I$. Choose $s_i>0$ tending to zero and regular points $p_i$. Set
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:rescaled-metrics}
 \widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i&=&s_i^{-2}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,
 \qquad h_i=s_i^{-2}\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,\nonumber\\
 \widetilde\rho_i&=&s_i^{-2}\rho_i,
 \qquad \varepsilon_i=\lambda s_i^2.
\end{eqnarray}
Then $\text{Ric}(\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)=\varepsilon_i\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i$. Assume that
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:curvature-normalization}
 |\text{Rm}(\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}&\leq&2,
 \qquad
 |\text{Rm}(\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i)=1.
\end{eqnarray}
<!-- end notation-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:rescaled-covers}
For a sequence as in Notation~\ref{not:rescaled-covers}, put $b_i:=\pi(p_i)$ and write $c_i$ for the conical point. All distances and balls below are taken in $h_i$. Pass to a subsequence so that the distances from $b_i$ to $c_i$ and to each axis are either bounded or tend to infinity. Choose $R_i\to\infty$ so that every escaping axis or cone lies outside $B_{h_i}(b_i,2R_i)$ and
\[
\varepsilon_iV_{2,-2}(4R_i+1)\longrightarrow0,
\qquad V_{2,-2}(r):=\pi\bigl(\cosh(\sqrt2r)-1\bigr).
\]
Here $V_{2,-2}(r)$ is the area of a radius-$r$ ball in the hyperbolic plane of curvature $-2$.

Choose a connected relatively open domain $\mathcal Q_i\subset\Sigma$ with piecewise smooth boundary such that
\[
B_{h_i}(b_i,R_i)\subset\mathcal Q_i\subset B_{h_i}(b_i,2R_i).
\]
In a fixed planar realization of $\Sigma$, let $\operatorname{Fill}(\mathcal Q_i)$ be obtained by filling the bounded complementary components. Set
\[
\mathcal Q_i^+:=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal Q_i, & d_{h_i}(b_i,c_i)\to\infty,\\
\operatorname{Fill}(\mathcal Q_i)\cup\{c_i\}, & \sup_i d_{h_i}(b_i,c_i)<\infty,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\mathcal Q_i^*:=\mathcal Q_i^+\cap\bigl(\Sigma^\circ\setminus\{c_i\}\bigr).
\]
Put $U_i:=\pi^{-1}(\mathcal Q_i^+)$. Its \emph{partially unwrapped cover} $\widehat U_i$ is the metric completion of the universal cover of the underlying manifold $U_i$, including the axes and the conical orbit when present. Choose a lift $\widehat p_i$ of $p_i$ and also write $\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i$ for the lifted metric.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:short-axis}
Let $K_i$ be a fixed primitive circle generator of a diagonal metric $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i$ with $|\mathrm{Rm}|\leq2$, and suppose $Z_i:=\{K_i=0\}$ is smooth. For a fixed $D>0$, assume $B_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,2D+1)$ is smooth and $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,Z_i)\leq D$. If $|K_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i)\to0$, then $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,Z_i)\to0$. If both fixed generators $K_{i,1},K_{i,2}$ satisfy these hypotheses and their lengths at $p_i$ tend to zero, then $d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,\{K_{i,1}=K_{i,2}=0\})\to0$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
The time-$t$ flow of $K_i$ rotates the normal plane to $Z_i$ through angle $t$, so $|\nabla K_i|^2=2$ on $Z_i$. Integrating $|\nabla^2K_i|\leq C|K_i|$ along curves of length at most $L$ starting on $Z_i$ gives
\begin{equation*}
 \sqrt2e^{-CL}
 \leq (|K_i|^2+|\nabla K_i|^2)^{1/2}
 \leq \sqrt2e^{CL},
\end{equation*}
with $C$ independent of $i$. Choose a unit-speed minimizing geodesic $\gamma_i$ from $Z_i$ to $p_i$. Set $l_i:=d_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,Z_i)$ and $j_i(t):=|K_i(\gamma_i(t))|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}$. The diagonal form gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:primitive-jacobi-data}
 j_i''+\mathrm{Sec}_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(\dot\gamma_i,K_i)j_i=0,
 \qquad j_i(0)=0,\qquad j_i'(0)=1.
\end{equation}
Suppose $l_i\geq d>0$ and pass to a subsequence with $l_i\to l\in[d,D]$. Extend $\gamma_i$ beyond $p_i$ by $d/2$. A zero on this extension would lie within distance $d/2<l_i$ of $p_i$, contradicting the definition of $l_i$. Thus $j_i>0$ on $(0,l_i+d/2]$. The bound $|j_i''|\leq2j_i$ gives, after a further subsequence, $\mathcal C^1$ convergence on $[0,l+d/4]$ to a nonnegative function $j$. Since $j_i(l_i)\to0$, we have $j(l)=j'(l)=0$. The limit satisfies $|j''|\leq2j$ almost everywhere, so Gronwall's inequality gives $j\equiv0$, contradicting $j'(0)=1$. Choose $q_i\in Z_{i,1}$ with $d(p_i,q_i)\to0$. The uniform gradient bound gives $|K_{i,2}|(q_i)\to0$. Commutation makes $K_{i,2}$ tangent to $Z_{i,1}$ and, together with orthogonality, gives $\nabla_{K_{i,1}}K_{i,2}=0$. Differentiating on $Z_{i,1}$, where $\nabla K_{i,1}$ rotates the normal plane, gives $\nabla_\nu K_{i,2}=0$ for every normal vector $\nu$. The preceding lower bound therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
 |\nabla^{Z_{i,1}}K_{i,2}|(q_i)
 =|\nabla K_{i,2}|(q_i)\geq c>0
\end{equation*}
for all sufficiently large $i$, with $c$ independent of $i$. Set $A_i:=\nabla^{Z_{i,1}}K_{i,2}(q_i)$. Since $A_i$ is skew on a two-dimensional plane, $\|A_i^{-1}\|\leq C$. In exponential coordinates on $Z_{i,1}$ and a radial parallel frame, write $K_{i,2}$ as $F_i(y)$. Jacobi comparison and the Killing identity give
\begin{equation*}
 \sup_{|y|\leq r}\|DF_i(y)-A_i\|\leq Cr,
\end{equation*}
uniformly in $i$. For fixed sufficiently small $r$, the quantitative inverse function theorem gives $F_i(y_i)=0$ with $|y_i|\leq C|F_i(0)|=C|K_{i,2}|(q_i)$. The exponential disk need only be immersed. Thus $z_i:=\exp_{q_i}(y_i)$ is a common zero, and $d(p_i,z_i)\leq d(p_i,q_i)+C|K_{i,2}|(q_i)\to0$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:retained-period-volume}
Consider the covers of Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers}, and suppose that $d_{\tilde \ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i, \mathcal T) \to \infty$. If the reflected quotient has injectivity radius bounded below on fixed balls and each retained primitive circle has an axis at uniformly bounded distance from the basepoint, then unit balls centered in any fixed pointed ball have volume bounded below.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Write $N_a=|K_a|$ and suppose $\operatorname{Vol}B(x_i,1)\to0$ for centers in a fixed pointed ball. The transport estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:short-axis} uniformly bounds $N_a$ and $\ensuremath{\text{d}} N_a$ for each circle retained in the cover. After passage to a subsequence, each $N_a(x_i)$ tends to zero or stays bounded below. If $N_a(x_i)\to0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:short-axis} gives $d(x_i,Z_a)\to0$; if both $N_a(x_i)$ tend to zero, $x_i$ approaches a common zero of the generators. A retained circle that is not short has uniformly comparable length on a smaller fixed ball. Normalize each unwrapped direction at the center; \eqref{eq:positive-jacobi-bound} gives the same comparability there.

Near a point where neither generator vanishes, use a quotient rectangle and two orbit intervals. Near one axis, use a polar disk and two intervals; near a common zero, use two polar disks. The reflected-quotient injectivity makes the corresponding quotient normal or Fermi neighborhood embedded at a fixed radius. Jacobi comparison controls its metric, and \eqref{eq:primitive-jacobi-data} gives $N_a(r)=r+O(r^3)$ along each collapsing radius. Choose every remaining orbit interval to have a fixed length in the rescaled metric. The lower bound for $N_a$ allows this interval to fit within a retained period; a direction lifted to a line has no period restriction. Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers} leaves no further orbit identifications and retains the full $2\pi$ period of each collapsed circle. Integrating $N_1N_2\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} v_h\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_1\,\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta_2$, the volume form in~\eqref{eq:orbit-volume}, gives a positive lower bound in every model. Choose their radii uniformly small enough that these regions lie in $B(x_i,1)$. Their positive volume lower bound contradicts $\operatorname{Vol}B(x_i,1)\to0$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:uniform-cone-estimates}
Suppose $W_i$ is uniformly bounded in $x^\delta\mathcal C_b^{2,\alpha}(D)$. On a fixed smaller disk $D'$, we have
\[
\sup_i\|W_i\|_{x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')}<\infty
\]
for every $m$, $0<\alpha'<1$, and $0<\delta'<\min\{1,2\beta_0\}$. If also $\beta_i\to\beta_\infty$, $\varepsilon_i\to0$, and the normalized coefficients converge locally in $\mathcal C^2$ off $x=0$ to those of a flat product cone, then $|\text{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(q_i)\to 0$ for every sequence of regular points with $x(q_i)\to0$.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
These local rescalings give $W_i\to0$ as $x\to0$. We record the original periods of the primitive circle generators separately. Setting $x=as$ maps $a<x<2a$ to $1<s<2$ and changes the principal part of \eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} to $(s\partial_s)^2+\partial_\vartheta^2$. Schauder estimates~\cite[Theorem~6.2]{GilbargTrudinger}, applied to the equations and their derivatives, give
\begin{equation*}
 \sup_i\|W_i\|_{x^\delta\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')}<\infty
\end{equation*}
for every $m$, on a fixed smaller disk $D'$. Set $\rho_i:=e^{f_i}$. With Einstein constant $\varepsilon_i$, the first equation of \eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} becomes
\begin{equation*}
 \Delta_b\rho_i =-2\varepsilon_i x^{2\beta_i}e^{2v_i}\rho_i.
\end{equation*}
Fix $0<\delta'<\min\{1,2\beta_0\}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier-estimate} gives $\rho_i-1,f_i\in x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')$, with uniform bounds. Since $\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_i,\ensuremath{\text{d}} u_i\rangle_b \in x^{\delta+\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')$ with uniformly bounded norm, the same proposition applied to the $u_i$ equation gives $\sup_i\|u_i\|_{x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')}<\infty$. Hence $\tfrac14(|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_i|_b^2-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u_i|_b^2) \in x^{2\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')$ with uniform bounds. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier-estimate} then gives $v_i\in x^{\delta'}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha}(D')$, also with uniform bounds. Choose $\delta'<\eta<\min\{1,2\beta_0\}$ and repeat these estimates at weight $\eta$. The inclusion $x^\eta\mathcal C_b^{m+1,\alpha}(D') \subset x^{\delta'}c_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:decay-implies-little})  gives
\begin{equation*}
\sup_i\|W_i\|_{x^{\delta'}c_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')}<\infty, \qquad 0<\alpha'<1.
\end{equation*}

We now prove the curvature convergence assertion. Choose $\beta_-<\beta_\infty<a_0<\min\{1,2\beta_-\}$. Discard finitely many indices so that $\beta_-\leq\beta_i\leq(\beta_\infty+a_0)/2$. Applying the first part to this tail with lower angle bound $\beta_-$ gives $\sup_i\|W_i\|_{x^{a_0}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')}<\infty$ for every $m$. Thus, for $0<x<1$,
\begin{equation*}
|\ensuremath{\text{d}} W_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}\leq Cx^{a_0-\beta_i}  \leq Cx^{(a_0-\beta_\infty)/2}\longrightarrow0
\end{equation*}
uniformly in $i$ as $x\to0$. Set $r_i:=x^{\beta_i}/\beta_i$ and $H_i:=W_i+\tfrac12\varepsilon_i(r_i^2,0,0)$. Since $\Delta_b r_i^2=4x^{2\beta_i}$, \eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \Delta_b(H_i)_f
 &=&\Delta_b f_i+2\varepsilon_i x^{2\beta_i}\\
 &=&-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_b}^2
     -2\varepsilon_i x^{2\beta_i}(e^{2v_i}-1).
\end{eqnarray*}
Together with the other two equations of \eqref{eq:scalar-b-system}, this gives $\sup_i\|\Delta_bH_i\|_{x^{2a_0}\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')}<\infty$ for every $m$. Set $N_{i,\pm}:=e^{(f_i\pm u_i)/2}$. For a unit horizontal vector $\xi$, the plane spanned by $\xi$ and the corresponding circle direction has sectional curvature $-N_{i,\pm}^{-1}\nabla_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}^2N_{i,\pm}(\xi,\xi)$. The plane tangent to the torus orbit has sectional curvature $-\langle\ensuremath{\text{d}}\log N_{i,+},\ensuremath{\text{d}}\log N_{i,-}\rangle_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}$. Equation~\eqref{eqn:red-einstein-3} gives $4K_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} u_i|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}^2-|\ensuremath{\text{d}} f_i|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}^2$. Combining this with the preceding curvature formulas and the Hessian formula for $\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i=e^{2v_i}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}$ gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
 |\text{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}
 &\leq&C\bigl(
 |\nabla_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2 f_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}
 +|\nabla_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2 u_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}
 +|\ensuremath{\text{d}} W_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2\bigr),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $C$ is independent of $i$. If $\beta_\infty<1/2$, choose $2\beta_\infty<a<\min\{1,2a_0\}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier-estimate} gives $\sup_i\|H_i\|_{x^a\mathcal C_b^{m,\alpha'}(D')}<\infty$ for every $m$. Hence
\begin{equation*}
 |\nabla_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2f_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}
 +|\nabla_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2u_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}
 \leq C\bigl(|\varepsilon_i|+x^{a-2\beta_i}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Since $\varepsilon_i\to0$ and $a>2\beta_\infty$, the right-hand side tends to zero at $q_i$. If $\beta_\infty=1/2$, choose $1<b<\min\{2,2a_0\}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier-estimate} gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
 f_i+\tfrac12\varepsilon_i r_i^2
 &=&x\ell_{i,f}+R_{i,f},\\
 u_i&=&x\ell_{i,u}+R_{i,u},
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\ell_{i,f},\ell_{i,u}\in \text{span}\{\cos\vartheta,\sin\vartheta\}$ and $\sup_i\|(R_{i,f},R_{i,u})\|_{x^b\mathcal C_b^2(D')}<\infty$. Flatness of the limit and the mixed sectional curvature formula give $\nabla_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty}^2N_{\infty,\pm}=0$. Since $|\ensuremath{\text{d}} N_{\infty,\pm}|_{\hat\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty}\to0$ as $x\to0$, their vanishing Hessians and the normalization give $N_{\infty,\pm}\equiv1$. Thus $f_\infty=u_\infty=0$. For each fixed $x>0$, the expansions give
\begin{equation*}
 \limsup_{i\to\infty}
 \bigl(\|\ell_{i,f}\|_{L^\infty(S^1)}
       +\|\ell_{i,u}\|_{L^\infty(S^1)}\bigr)
 \leq Cx^{b-1}.
\end{equation*}
Letting $x\downarrow0$ gives $\ell_{i,f},\ell_{i,u}\to0$. For $\ell\in\text{span}\{\cos\vartheta,\sin\vartheta\}$, differentiation in the orthonormal frame $(x^{1-\beta}\partial_x,x^{-\beta}\partial_\vartheta)$ gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \nabla^2_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\beta}(x\ell)
 &=&(1-\beta)x^{1-2\beta}
 \begin{pmatrix}
  \ell&\partial_\vartheta\ell\\
  \partial_\vartheta\ell&-\ell
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{eqnarray*}
For $0<x\leq1$, $\beta_i\leq1/2$ gives $x^{1-2\beta_i}\leq1$ and $x^{b-2\beta_i}\leq x^{b-1}$. The preceding estimates therefore give
\begin{eqnarray*}
 |\text{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}
 &\leq&C\bigl(
 \|\ell_{i,f}\|_{L^\infty(S^1)}
 +\|\ell_{i,u}\|_{L^\infty(S^1)}\\
 &&\qquad+x^{b-1}+|\varepsilon_i|
 +|\ensuremath{\text{d}} W_i|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_{\beta_i}}^2\bigr).
\end{eqnarray*}
At $q_i$, every term on the right tends to zero. Hence $|\text{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i)|_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(q_i)\to0$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-isothermal}
Suppose the Beltrami coefficients $\mu_i$ on a disk satisfy $\mu_i=O_b^1(|z|^\sigma)$ uniformly, with $\sigma>0$. For every $0<q<\min\{1,\sigma\}$, a common smaller disk has isothermal coordinates $\zeta_i=z+O_b^{1,\alpha}(|z|^{1+q})$, for every $0<\alpha<1$.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
For compactly supported $\eta$, define the Cauchy transform and the Beurling transform by
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \mathcal C\eta(z)&=&\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{\eta(\xi)}{z-\xi}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A(\xi),\\
 S\eta(z)&=&\partial_z\mathcal C\eta(z)
 =-\frac1\pi\operatorname{p.v.}\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{\eta(\xi)}{(z-\xi)^2}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A(\xi).
\end{eqnarray*}
Cut off $\mu_i$ on a small disk and choose $p>2$ with $2/p<\sigma-q$. Shrink the support until $\|\mu_i\|_\infty\|S\|_{L^p\to L^p}<1/2$. The construction in~\cite[Lemmas~3--5 and Theorem~4]{AhlforsBers} gives $\eta_i=\mu_i(1+S\eta_i)$ and $\phi_i=z+\mathcal C\eta_i$, with uniform $L^p$ bounds; Lemma~8 of the same paper implies that $\phi_i$ is a homeomorphism. Since $\eta_i=\mu_i(1+S\eta_i)$ and $\sigma-2/p>q$, H\"older's inequality makes the following integral convergent:
\begin{eqnarray*}
 A_i=1-\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{\eta_i(\xi)}{\xi^2}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A(\xi).
\end{eqnarray*}
Subtracting the constant and linear terms gives
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \phi_i(z)-\phi_i(0)-A_iz
 =\frac{z^2}\pi\int_{\mathbb C}
 \frac{\eta_i(\xi)}{\xi^2(z-\xi)}\,\ensuremath{\text{d}} A(\xi).
\end{eqnarray*}
Splitting this integral into $|\xi|\leq2|z|$ and $|\xi|>2|z|$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:isothermal-first-jet}
 \phi_i(z)-\phi_i(0)=A_iz+O(|z|^{1+q}),
 \qquad |A_i-1|<\tfrac12,
\end{equation}
after a further uniform shrinking. Writing $z=aw$ on $a<|z|<2a$, the coefficients $\mu_i(aw)$ have uniformly bounded Lipschitz norms on $1<|w|<2$. Interior Beltrami estimates~\cite[Chapter~15]{AstalaIwaniecMartin2009} therefore give $D\phi_i-A_i=O_b^{0,\alpha}(|z|^q)$. Taking $\zeta_i=(\phi_i-\phi_i(0))/A_i$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:normalized-cone-charts}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i\in\mathcal X_{\beta_i}$ be Einstein, with $\beta_i\in I$, and suppose $\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i=s_i^{-2}\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i$ have uniformly bounded curvature. Then $(\Sigma,h_i)$ admit injective geodesic polar coordinates of uniform radius about $c_i$, together with normalized isothermal charts satisfying the uniform weighted estimates of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-cone-estimates}.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
After a fixed rescaling take the curvature bound to be $2$, and write $h_i$ and $\varepsilon_i>0$ for the quotient metrics and Einstein constants. We first construct the geodesics issuing from $c_i$. On a sector with Cartesian coordinate $y=r_{\beta_i}e^{i\beta_i\vartheta}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:cone-regularity} gives $h_i=|\ensuremath{\text{d}} y|^2+O_b(|y|^2)$. Its Cartesian coefficients extend in $\mathcal C^{1,1}$ to the vertex, with Christoffel symbols $O(|y|)$ and bounded first derivatives. The locally Lipschitz geodesic equation therefore gives a unique curve in each initial direction. For $\eta>0$, solve the geodesic equation with $y(\eta)=\eta e^{i\beta_i\vartheta}$ and $y'(\eta)=e^{i\beta_i\vartheta}$. Pass to the limit as $\eta\downarrow0$ in the integral equation and its derivatives with respect to $\vartheta$. Angular differentiation is justified inductively: the $m$th Cartesian derivatives of the Christoffel symbols are $O(|y|^{1-m})$, while each angular variation is $O(t)$, so the differentiated terms remain integrable. The resulting family is smooth for $t>0$. Gauss' lemma gives the angular Jacobi factor $j_i=\beta_it+O(t^3)$ and $(j_i)_t=\beta_i+O(t^2)$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-curvature} and \eqref{eqn:general-horizontal}, $\nabla^2f\leq-2\varepsilon_i h_i/3$. Normalize $N_a(c_i)=1$. Mixed curvature gives $|\nabla^2N_a|\leq2N_a$ and $\ensuremath{\text{d}} N_a(c_i)=0$, so $N_a(t)\geq\cos(\sqrt2t)$. Every axis is therefore at distance at least $\pi/(2\sqrt2)$ from the cone. The Jacobi equation with $j_i(0)=0$ and $(j_i)_t(0)=\beta_i$ excludes conjugacy before $\pi/\sqrt2$.

Fix $t_0$ below both radii. Along every geodesic leaving $c_i$, we have $f'(0)=0$ and $f''\leq-2\varepsilon_i/3$; integration forbids a return to $c_i$. Thus the radial family extends to $t_0$, since it can meet neither an axis nor the cone. If two radial geodesics first met at a regular point at distance $l<t_0$, the absence of conjugate points would make the radial exponential map a local diffeomorphism near each preimage. The images of the neighborhoods $t<l$ are disjoint, so their inward tangent half-planes are disjoint. In two dimensions this forces exactly two preimages with opposite terminal tangents. Joining the two geodesics gives a geodesic of length $2l$ from $c_i$ to itself, contradicting the preceding concavity argument. The exclusion of a return to $c_i$ uses positivity of $\varepsilon_i$, with no uniform lower bound. The polar disk of radius $t_0$ is therefore injective without a volume estimate.

To obtain isothermal coordinates, write $h_i=\ensuremath{\text{d}} t^2+j_i^2\ensuremath{\text{d}}\vartheta^2$. Radial integration of the mixed-curvature bound gives $N_a-1=O(t^2)$, with gradient $O(t)$ and Hessian $O(1)$. Equation~\eqref{eqn:red-einstein-3} then gives $K_h=O(t^2)$ and $|\ensuremath{\text{d}} K_h|=O(t)$. Since $|\partial_\vartheta|=j_i=O(t)$, it also gives $\partial_\vartheta K_h=O(t^2)$. Differentiating the Jacobi equation with initial data $j_i(0)=0$ and $(j_i)_t(0)=\beta_i$ yields $j_i/(\beta_it)=1+O(t^4)$; the radial and angular derivatives of this ratio are respectively $O(t^3)$ and $O(t^4)$.

Put $z=(\beta_it)^{1/\beta_i}e^{i\vartheta}$ and $x=|z|$. The preceding Jacobi bounds give $\mu_i=O_b^1(x^{4\beta_i})$. Choose $\delta<q<\min\{1,2\beta_0\}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-isothermal} gives normalized isothermal coordinates $\zeta_i$ on a common disk; write $\zeta=\zeta_i$ in the formulas below. Then $h_i=|\zeta|^{2\beta_i-2}e^{2v_i}|\ensuremath{\text{d}}\zeta|^2$ and $v_i=O_b^{0,\alpha}(|\zeta|^q)$. The mixed-curvature bounds give $f_i,u_i=O_b^{1,\alpha}(|\zeta|^{2\beta_i})$. Applying annular Schauder estimates~\cite[Theorem~6.2]{GilbargTrudinger} to~\eqref{eq:scalar-b-system} yields the initial $|\zeta|^q\mathcal C_b^{2,\alpha}$ bounds; Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-cone-estimates} then supplies the higher bounds.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:reflected-quotient-injectivity}
For the covers of Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers}, suppose the conical orbit escapes. Then the reflected quotient has injectivity radius bounded below on every fixed pointed ball.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Use the reflected quotient defined after Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers}. Fixed-radius balls in this smooth surface have compact closure and remain away from the artificial boundary. A geodesic segment of length $l<\pi/\sqrt2$ cannot meet the same axis twice unless it lies in that axis. Indeed, the ambient Jacobi field $J=K_a|_\gamma$ vanishes at the two intersections, and in a parallel frame
\[
 (\pi/l)^2\int|J|^2\leq\int|D_tJ|^2
 =\int\langle\mathrm{Rm}(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma,J\rangle
 \leq2\int|J|^2.
\]
Thus $J=0$. A short geodesic loop based off the axes therefore crosses each axis at most once. A crossing changes the corresponding orbit angle by $\pi$, whereas retained periods are $2\pi$; closure forces no crossings. If the basepoint lies on an axis, the same Jacobi argument confines the loop to that axis. Within the reflected section, the axis is a smooth one-dimensional manifold. A geodesic on it cannot reverse direction, so a return to its initial point gives a smoothly closed geodesic. If this geodesic met a corner, start its parametrization there and apply the same inequality to the other generator. Both generators would then vanish along the entire loop, contrary to the isolated nature of their common zeros. The loop therefore stays in an open edge interval, where it cannot close. Every short geodesic loop consequently lies in a single principal chamber, which is simply connected by the observation following Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers}.

If the reflected quotient injectivity radius tended to zero, the conjugate-radius bound and the local geodesic-loop alternative~\cite[p.~45]{CheegerGromovTaylor} would produce arbitrarily short loops. If such a loop has self-intersections, choose a subarc of smallest positive length whose endpoints agree. This minimum is positive because a geodesic is locally injective on its compact parameter interval. The subarc has embedded interior and is geodesic away from its new basepoint. We thus obtain a simple geodesic loop of length $L_i<1$, which bounds a disk $F$ in its simply connected chamber. Every point of $F$ can be joined to the artificial boundary by a path of length at most $4R_i$: project to $\mathcal Q_i^+$, follow a minimizing path towards the basepoint, and, if it stays in the domain, continue towards the excluded cone until the first exit. Lift this path from the chosen point. It exits the compact disk $F$ before reaching the artificial boundary, so the inradius of $F$ is at most $D_i=4R_i$.

To estimate the area without assuming injectivity, cover $F$, up to its cut locus, by inward normals from its geodesic boundary and the inward sector at its vertex. Comparison with curvature $-2$ bounds their Jacobians, and the sector angle is at most $2\pi$. Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:loop-disk-area}
 \operatorname{Area}(F)\leq
 \frac{L_i}{\sqrt2}\sinh(\sqrt2D_i)
 +\pi\bigl(\cosh(\sqrt2D_i)-1\bigr)
 \leq C V_{2,-2}(4R_i+1).
\end{equation}
Gauss--Bonnet gives $\int_FK_{h_i} = \pi + \alpha_i \geq\pi$ for a simple geodesic loop, where $\alpha_i \geq 0$ is the interior angle at the loop basepoint. Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-curvature}, \eqref{eq:loop-disk-area}, and Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers} give the contradiction:
\begin{eqnarray*}
\pi\leq\int_FK_{h_i}
\leq\frac{\varepsilon_i}{3}\text{Area}(F)
\leq C\varepsilon_iV_{2,-2}(4R_i+1)\longrightarrow0.
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:covered-local-bounds}
For every $A>0$, there exists $v_A>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $i$,
\[
\operatorname{Vol}  B_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(x,1)\geq v_A,
\qquad\text{for every }x\in B_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(\widehat p_i,A)\subset\widehat U_i.
\]
On $B_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(\widehat p_i,A)$, the lifted metrics admit uniform smooth local coefficient bounds at any fixed positive distance from the conical orbit. When that orbit is present, they also satisfy the weighted bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-cone-estimates} in normalized cone charts.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Suppose first that the cone remains at bounded distance. Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-cone-charts} supplies its normalized chart. A retained generator has an axis at bounded distance, where $|\nabla K_a|=\sqrt2$. The transport estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:short-axis} gives $|K_a|(c_i)\geq c>0$, since the first derivatives of the orbit metric coefficients vanish at $c_i$. Normalize only unwrapped directions. The polar disk times a fixed orbit rectangle is then uniformly comparable to a product cone with $\beta\geq\beta_0$. This gives a volume lower bound on a fixed cone neighbourhood. Local volume comparison propagates it along paths of bounded length; portions meeting the cone are covered by the same uniform product-cone charts. Thus, for each $A$,
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{eq:cone-local-volume}
\text{Vol}_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}B(x,a)&\geq&c_Aa^4,
\qquad x\in B(\widehat p_i,A),\quad 0<a<a_A.
\end{eqnarray}

If the cone escapes, Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected-quotient-injectivity} bounds the reflected-quotient injectivity radius below. Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers} retains precisely the fixed circles whose axes stay at bounded distance. Lemma~\ref{lem:retained-period-volume} therefore gives noncollapse of the four-dimensional lift.

On each fixed smooth ball, take the comparison radius below its distance to the cone and to the artificial boundary. Noncollapse now permits the local injectivity estimate \cite[Theorem~4.3]{CheegerGromovTaylor}; harmonic coordinates and Einstein regularity then give smooth local bounds \cite[Chapter~11]{petersen2016riemannian}, \cite[Theorem~5.2]{DeTurckKazdan1981}. For retained primitive generators, the transport estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:short-axis} bounds their first jets. Normalize each unwrapped generator at $\widehat p_i$ and use~\eqref{eq:positive-jacobi-bound} for the same bound. Differentiating the Killing identity then bounds all their derivatives in these charts. The ambient estimates apply also across axes and corners, which are smooth points of the lifted metrics. Lemma~\ref{lem:slice-regularity} and the expansions~\eqref{eqn:edge-slice-expansion}--\eqref{eqn:vertex-slice-expansion} then give uniform bounds for the coefficients in quotient and orbit coordinates. Together with the conical charts above, these are the required bounds.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:marked-compactness}
After passing to a subsequence, $(\widehat U_i,\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,\widehat p_i)$ converges to a complete pointed limit $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty,p_\infty)$ whose regular part is Ricci flat. The convergence is smooth away from the conical orbit, if present, and holds in the normalized weighted coefficients near that orbit.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:covered-local-bounds} gives noncollapse and uniform local coordinates. Smooth pointed compactness applies away from the cone \cite[Chapter~11]{petersen2016riemannian}. At the cone, Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-cone-estimates} improves the weight and differentiability; Lemma~\ref{lem:compactness} then gives convergence in the prescribed little H\"older norm. A diagonal subsequence joins these local limits. The artificial boundaries escape to infinity, so the completed limit is complete. It is Ricci flat because $\varepsilon_i\to0$. The limiting orbit fields are Killing and orthogonal. The fixed orbit coordinates retain the circle periods or line parameters chosen in Definition~\ref{def:rescaled-covers}.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:noedgebubble}
For a sequence as in Notation~\ref{not:rescaled-covers}, we have $d_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i,\mathcal T)\to\infty$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Suppose the conical orbit remains at bounded distance. On $\widehat U_i$, set $\psi_i:=\widetilde\rho_i/\widetilde\rho_i(c_i)$, viewing the quotient functions as pulled back to the cover. Lemma~\ref{lem:density-maximum} and~\eqref{eqn:general-trace} give
\[
0\leq\psi_i\leq1,\qquad \psi_i(c_i)=1,\qquad
\Delta_{h_i}\psi_i+2\varepsilon_i\psi_i=0.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:marked-compactness}, these functions converge to a harmonic function $\psi$ on the limiting quotient, with $\psi(c_\infty)=1$. In an isothermal coordinate, $\psi$ is bounded and Euclidean harmonic off the puncture, so it extends harmonically across it. The strong maximum principle gives $\psi\equiv1$.

Thus $df=0$, and~\eqref{eqn:general-horizontal} reduces to
\[
K_hh=\tfrac12\,du\otimes du.
\]
Comparing ranks yields $K_h=0$ and $du=0$, so the limit is a flat product cone. This contradicts~\eqref{eq:curvature-normalization}, by smooth convergence if the $\hat p_i$'s stay at a uniform positive distance from the cone, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-cone-estimates} if they approach it.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lem:free-section-displacements}
Suppose $(\widehat U_i,\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,\widehat p_i)$ converges smoothly to a connected complete smooth limit $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty,p)$. Let $\eta_i$ be fixed-point-free isometries of the covering interiors, commuting with the orbit flows and preserving each reflected section and its orientation. If $d_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(\widehat p_i,\eta_i(\widehat p_i))\to0$, then $X$ admits a nowhere-zero horizontal Killing field whose orthogonal distribution is integrable.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Move $\widehat p_i$ onto one section by an orbit translation. Since $\eta_i(B(\widehat p_i,R))\subset B(\widehat p_i,R+d(\widehat p_i,\eta_i\widehat p_i))$, the image of each fixed-radius ball lies in a slightly larger fixed-radius ball for all sufficiently large $i$. Smooth compactness of isometries follows from
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:isometry-first-jet}
 \eta_i(\exp_xv)=\exp_{\eta_ix}(\ensuremath{\text{d}}\eta_i|_xv).
\end{equation}
Apply it also to the inverses to obtain an onto limiting isometry $\eta$ fixing $p$. The sections converge as exponential images of their tangent planes. On the limiting section, $\ensuremath{\text{d}}\eta|_p$ is an orientation-preserving linear isometry. A non-identity rotation would give a nondegenerate fixed point, which persists for $\eta_i$, contrary to freeness. Thus \eqref{eq:isometry-first-jet} makes $\eta$ the identity near $p$ on the section. Commutation with the orbit flows makes it the identity on a principal open set, hence everywhere.

Set $V_i(x)=\exp_x^{-1}(\eta_ix)$ and $a_i=|j^1_{\widehat p_i}V_i|>0$, where the first-jet norm is $(|V_i|^2+|\nabla V_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Then $a_i\to0$. On a normal ball, \eqref{eq:isometry-first-jet} determines $\eta_i$ smoothly from its value and differential at the center. Their deviation from the identity is uniformly comparable to the value and derivative of $V_i$ there. Applying the mean-value theorem to this dependence, then covering $B(\widehat p_i,R)$ by finitely many overlapping normal balls, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:displacement-jet-bound}
 \|V_i\|_{C^j(B(\widehat p_i,R))}\leq C_{R,j}a_i.
\end{equation}
Thus $a_i^{-1}V_i\to Z$ smoothly, with $|j^1_pZ|=1$. Dividing $\eta_i^*\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i-\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i=0$ by $a_i$ proves that $Z$ is Killing. Naturality of the exponential map makes $V_i$ orbit-invariant. The two orbit-coordinate reversals fix $x$ and $\eta_ix$, hence also their unique short geodesic;  $V_i$ is tangent to every reflected section, including those through axes and corners. Hence $Z$ is horizontal and orbit-invariant.

If $Z(q)=0$, its restriction to the reflected section through $q$ is a nontrivial Killing field: otherwise orbit invariance would make $Z$ vanish on a principal open set. Its derivative at $q$ is a nonzero skew map in dimension two, so its zero is nondegenerate. Smooth convergence in~\eqref{eq:displacement-jet-bound} makes that zero persist for $a_i^{-1}V_i$, giving a fixed point of $\eta_i$. Thus $Z$ never vanishes. On the principal set $Z^\flat$ is pulled back from the two-dimensional quotient, so $Z^\flat\wedge\ensuremath{\text{d}} Z^\flat=0$; continuity extends this identity everywhere.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:no-collapsed-smooth-limit}
For a sequence as in Notation~\ref{not:rescaled-covers}, we have $\inf_i\operatorname{inj}_{\tilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i)>0$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:noedgebubble} and Lemma~\ref{lem:marked-compactness}, a subsequence of $(\widehat U_i,\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i,\widehat p_i)$ converges to a complete smooth Ricci-flat limit $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty,p)$ with $|\mathrm{Rm}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_\infty)|(p)=1$. If a direction were unwrapped, its axis would escape. Normalize the generator of this line action to have unit length at $p_i$ and apply the estimates in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-marked-action}. Those estimates do not require periodicity and give a global nowhere-zero Killing field with integrable orthogonal distribution. Lemma~\ref{lem:properness-static-field} would force flatness. Thus neither orbit direction is unwrapped: both primitive generators retain their $2\pi$ periods on $\widehat U_i$.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that $\operatorname{inj}_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}(p_i)\to0$ along a subsequence. The curvature bound excludes nearby conjugate points, so the local geodesic-loop alternative~\cite[p.~45]{CheegerGromovTaylor} gives loops based at $p_i$ with lengths tending to zero. For large $i$, these loops lie in $U_i$, and their lifts to $\widehat U_i$ have distinct endpoints because the lifted metrics have uniformly positive injectivity radius near $\widehat p_i$. Thus their endpoints are $\widehat p_i$ and $\eta_i(\widehat p_i)$ for nontrivial, fixed-point-free deck transformations satisfying
\[
d_{\widetilde\ensuremath{\mathrm{g}}_i}\bigl(\widehat p_i,\eta_i(\widehat p_i)\bigr)\to0.
\]
